13200:
To renounce something means to formally and deliberately give it up, reject it, or turn away from it — often something you previously held, owned, claimed, or believed in. The act is almost always conscious, intentional, and final. It is not a casual letting go. It is a clear, decided declaration: "I am done with this, and I am saying so."

Think of it this way: if you simply stop doing something quietly, that is not renouncing. But if you stand up and declare, "I no longer want this, I no longer accept this, I am walking away from this" — that is renouncing.
The Three Qualities That Define Renouncing

To truly understand this word, remember that renouncing almost always has three qualities working together:

1. It is deliberate. You choose to do it. It is not something that happens to you. You make a firm, conscious decision.

2. It is formal or public in nature. You are not just privately changing your mind. You are declaring it — to others, to the world, or at least in an official sense. A renouncement is a statement, not just a feeling.

3. It carries a sense of permanence. When someone renounces something, they are not saying "maybe later" or "for now." They are saying "this is over." There is a finality to it.

Renounce is a flexible verb. You can renounce many kinds of things:

Rights, titles, and claims. A king who steps down from the throne and gives up all his royal power has renounced the crown. A person who officially gives up their legal claim to an inheritance has renounced that right.

Beliefs and ideologies. A person who was once part of an extremist group, but publicly declares they no longer believe in its ideas, has renounced those beliefs. A person who leaves their religion and officially declares they no longer follow it has renounced their faith.

Citizenship and identity. When someone officially gives up the citizenship of a country — through a legal process — they have renounced their citizenship. This is a real, formal, legal act many people go through.

Violence, harmful behavior, or a way of life. A former criminal who publicly declares they are leaving that life behind has renounced violence or crime. A monk who gives up all material possessions and worldly pleasures to live a spiritual life has renounced the material world.

Ties to a person or group. A person can renounce a family member, a political party, or an organization — meaning they publicly cut their connection to them and refuse to be associated any further.

Here are clear, everyday examples so you can see the word in action:

  • "After years of fighting, the rebel leader renounced violence and agreed to peace talks."
  • "She renounced her citizenship and moved abroad permanently."
  • "The prince renounced his claim to the throne so he could marry the woman he loved."
  • "He renounced his old lifestyle and devoted himself to helping others."
  • "The politician renounced all ties to the corrupt organization."
  • "She renounced her faith after years of doubt."

In every one of these sentences, notice the pattern: someone is giving up something meaningful, doing so deliberately, and making it known.
The Emotional Weight of This Word

Renouncing something is never small. The word carries weight. It implies that what is being given up actually mattered — that it was significant, real, and connected to you in some important way. You do not renounce something trivial. You renounce things that defined you, that you held power over, that you believed in, or that others expected you to keep.

This is why renouncing often involves courage, sacrifice, or pain. It is a turning point. Think of someone renouncing a powerful position, or renouncing a belief they held their whole life. These are not easy acts. The word quietly acknowledges that difficulty.
The Most Important Confusion to Avoid: Renounce vs. Denounce

These two words look and sound similar, but they mean very different things. Mixing them up is one of the most common mistakes people make.

Renounce is about yourself — you are giving something up. The action points inward. "I renounce this belief" means you are stepping away from it.

Denounce is about someone or something else — you are speaking against them, condemning them, or publicly calling them out. "She denounced the corrupt officials" means she criticized and accused them publicly.

A simple way to remember:

  • Renounce → you are releasing something of your own.
  • Denounce → you are declaring something wrong about others.
How Renounce Compares to Similar Words

Several words are close in meaning to renounce, but each has a slightly different flavor:

Relinquish means to give something up, but it is more neutral and does not require a public declaration. You relinquish control quietly. You renounce it with a statement.

Abandon means to leave something behind, often suddenly or without care. It focuses on the act of leaving, not the declaration. Renounce is more deliberate and principled.

Forsake means to give something up or leave someone behind, often with a sense of betrayal or deep loss. It is more emotional and literary. Renounce is more formal.

Disown means to refuse to acknowledge a connection — usually to a person, like a family member. Renounce is broader and can apply to beliefs, rights, and positions too.

Abdicate is specifically about giving up a throne or a position of high power and responsibility. Renounce can be used in that context too, but it is much wider in scope.

Resign is about formally leaving a job or role. Renounce goes deeper — it is not just about leaving a role but rejecting what that role stood for, or giving up a right entirely.
A Final Summary to Lock It In

Renounce means to formally, deliberately, and often publicly give up something you previously held — whether that is a right, a title, a belief, a relationship, a citizenship, or a way of life. It is a word of finality and declaration. It implies that something mattered, and that you are consciously choosing to walk away from it — and saying so out loud. It is not passive. It is not quiet. It is an act of decision, and often, an act of courage.
13201:
To renovate something means to take something old, worn-out, or outdated — usually a building or a room — and make it look and feel new or significantly better by doing substantial work on it.

The key idea is this: something already exists, it has aged or deteriorated, and you are bringing it back to a good or even improved condition.

They decided to renovate their old farmhouse before moving in.
What Kind of Work Does "Renovate" Involve?

Renovating is not a small, quick fix. It typically involves one or more of the following:

  • Repairing structural damage (fixing cracked walls, leaky roofs, broken floors)
  • Replacing old or broken parts (new windows, new pipes, new wiring)
  • Updating the look and feel (new paint, new tiles, new flooring)
  • Improving the layout or functionality of a space

You might renovate just one room, like a kitchen or a bathroom, or an entire building.
The Most Important Thing to Understand

Renovating is about working with something that already exists. You are not starting from zero. There is always a pre-existing structure — a house, a room, a building — that is being transformed.

Think of it like this: imagine an old, run-down apartment with peeling paint, cracked tiles, and broken cabinets. After renovation, the same apartment has fresh walls, polished floors, modern fittings, and everything in working order. It is still the same apartment — but it has been made new again.

It does not mean rebuilding from scratch. If you tear down an old building and construct a completely new one in its place, that is rebuilding or reconstruction — not renovation. Renovation always preserves the existing structure and works within it.

It does not mean a minor repair. If a pipe bursts and you fix just that pipe, you are repairing it, not renovating. Renovation implies a broader, more substantial upgrade.

It does not mean just redecorating. If you simply repaint the walls or hang new curtains, that is redecorating. Renovation goes deeper — it often involves structural or functional changes, not just cosmetic ones.

Renovate vs. Restore
Both words involve making something better. However, restore means to bring something back to its exact original condition — as it once was. Renovate means to make something better or more modern — it does not have to match the original. You restore a painting to its original colors. You renovate a kitchen to make it more functional and up-to-date.

Renovate vs. Refurbish
These words are very close in meaning. Refurbish is often used for smaller-scale updates — furniture, equipment, offices — and suggests cleaning, repairing, and polishing rather than deep structural work. Renovate tends to be used for larger spaces and implies more extensive work.

Renovate vs. Remodel
In everyday use, these are often used interchangeably. However, remodel specifically suggests changing the layout or structure of a space — for example, removing a wall to combine two rooms. Renovate is broader and does not necessarily imply changing the layout.

FormExample
Base formWe want to renovate the office.
Past tenseThey renovated the old library last year.
Present participleShe is renovating her apartment.
Third person singularHe renovates old houses for a living.
Noun (renovation)The renovation took six months.
Person who renovates (renovator)The renovator started work on Monday.

(Included this for completeness — not etymology or pronunciation.)

These are the natural phrases you will see "renovate" used in:

  • renovate a house / a home / an apartment
  • renovate a kitchen / a bathroom
  • renovate a building / a school / a hotel
  • completely / extensively / partially renovate
  • renovate from top to bottom (meaning every part of it)

Yes, occasionally. You might see it used beyond physical buildings to describe bringing new life to systems, organisations, or processes:

The new management team hopes to renovate the company's culture.

This usage is less common, but perfectly understood when you see it.

To renovate = to take something old or worn-down (usually a building or room) and do substantial work on it to make it look better, function better, or feel new again — without building it from scratch.
13202:
Renown means the state of being widely known and admired by many people — specifically because of something impressive, excellent, or worthy of respect.

It is not just fame. It is fame that has been earned through great skill, exceptional achievement, or outstanding quality. Think of it as a kind of glory that surrounds a person or thing when the world recognizes their greatness.

Imagine a doctor who has spent decades performing groundbreaking surgeries that no one else could. Over time, people all over the world — other doctors, patients, medical journals, governments — come to know about her and deeply respect her. That reputation, that widespread recognition of her greatness, is her renown.

So renown has two key ingredients:

  • Reach — a large number of people know about this person or thing.
  • Admiration — they don't just know about it, they respect and admire it.

Remove either ingredient, and it isn't quite renown anymore.

This is important, because English has many words that seem similar but mean different things.

Fame is the broad word. A serial killer can be famous. A person who accidentally went viral on the internet can be famous. Fame simply means many people know who you are — it carries no judgment about why.

Renown, however, is always positive. You cannot have renown for something shameful or trivial. A person of renown is someone the world looks up to. If someone is widely known for bad or disgraceful reasons, English speakers would use words like notoriety or infamy — never renown.

Celebrity is fame that tends to be shallow and tied to entertainment or pop culture. A reality TV star might be a celebrity but would not typically be described as having renown.

Renown carries a sense of substance and weight. It belongs to surgeons, great writers, celebrated scientists, master architects, legendary warriors, brilliant artists — people whose reputation is built on genuine excellence.
How It Feels in a Sentence

Renown is an uncountable noun, which means you cannot say "a renown" or "two renowns". You use it without an article, or you describe its degree.

Here is how it naturally appears:

  • "She is a scientist of great renown."

(Her greatness is widely recognized.)

  • "He gained renown as a poet."

(He earned his reputation through his poetry.)

  • "The hospital has international renown."

(People across the world know of and respect this hospital.)

  • "Her renown spread far beyond her own country."

(More and more of the world came to recognize her greatness.)

Notice the kinds of phrases renown pairs with: of great renown, of international renown, of worldwide renown, gained renown, achieved renown, earned renown.
The Register (When and Where It's Used)

Renown is a formal and slightly literary word. You will find it most often in:

  • Written language (books, articles, formal speeches)
  • Descriptions of historical or distinguished figures
  • Professional and academic contexts

In casual everyday conversation, people are more likely to say "famous" or "well-known." But when you want to express fame that carries dignity, weight, and genuine admiration — especially in writing — renown is the precise and powerful word to use.
The Adjective You Will Constantly See

Because it appears so frequently, you should also know that the adjective form is renowned, meaning having renown or famous and admired for excellence.

  • "She is a renowned surgeon." = She has renown as a surgeon.
  • "He is a world-renowned architect." = The whole world knows of and admires his work.

Renowned is actually used more frequently in everyday English than the noun renown, so recognizing both forms will help you enormously.

Renown is the fame and deep admiration that a person or thing earns from a wide audience — specifically because of genuine excellence, great achievement, or outstanding quality. It is always a positive kind of reputation, and it always implies that the recognition is deserved.
13203:
When you call someone or something renowned, you mean that they are widely known AND deeply respected or admired — specifically because of a particular skill, quality, or achievement. It is not just fame. It is fame that comes with genuine respect, earned through excellence.

Think of it this way: renowned = widely recognized + highly regarded + for a specific reason.
The Single Most Important Distinction: "Renowned" vs. "Famous"

This is the heart of the word, so pay close attention.

Famous simply means that many people know about you. It says nothing about why you are known or whether people admire you. A criminal can be famous. A scandal can be famous. Fame is neutral.

Renowned, however, carries weight and dignity. It means people don't just know of you — they look up to you or hold you in high regard because of a genuine achievement or outstanding quality. Renowned is fame with respect and admiration baked into it.

A brilliant surgeon who has saved thousands of lives is renowned. A reality TV star who went viral for doing something silly might be famous, but would not typically be called renowned.

Renowned sits at a very high level. It is not used for mild or local recognition. When someone is renowned, their reputation is strong, established, and typically known across a wide area — often nationally or internationally. It implies that the recognition is not accidental or temporary, but earned and lasting.

Think of it on a scale: known → well-known → respected → famous → renowned.

It is a word that carries a sense of prestige. If you describe someone as renowned, you are placing them among the genuinely exceptional.

Renowned has a purely positive connotation. You will never correctly use it to describe someone known for something bad or shameful. For that, English uses words like notorious (famous for something negative) or infamous (having a bad reputation). Renowned, by contrast, always signals admiration and high esteem.

One of the most natural and common ways renowned is used is with the word "for". This is because renowned almost always points to a specific reason for the recognition. The structure is:

[person/place/thing] + is renowned + for + [the reason]

For example:

  • She is renowned for her ability to negotiate impossible deals.
  • The city is renowned for its stunning architecture.
  • He is renowned for his generosity.

You will also see it used with "as" when describing someone's role or identity:

  • She is renowned as one of the finest violinists of her generation.

And it is very commonly paired with intensifiers like "world-renowned" or "internationally renowned" to stress just how wide the recognition is.

• Albert Einstein was a renowned physicist whose theories changed how we understand the universe. (He is widely recognized AND deeply respected for his scientific brilliance.)
  • The small bakery became renowned for its sourdough bread, drawing visitors from across the country. (Not just popular — admired and sought out for a specific excellence.)
  • She is a renowned human rights lawyer who has argued cases before the highest courts. (Her reputation is built on real achievement and commands respect.)
  • Harvard is a renowned university. (Known globally and admired for its academic standard.)
How It Compares to Similar Words

Several words are close to renowned but are not identical.

Celebrated is very similar and often interchangeable with renowned, but it tends to appear more in artistic or cultural contexts — a celebrated novelist, a celebrated painting. Renowned works more broadly across all fields.

Eminent suggests someone who has reached the very top of their field, often used in academic or professional settings — an eminent professor, an eminent scientist. It is slightly more formal and focuses more on professional standing than general public recognition.

Distinguished means someone who has been set apart from others by their excellence or achievements. It carries a sense of being noticeably superior, with a slightly more formal or old-fashioned feel.

Acclaimed means having received enthusiastic praise, usually from experts, critics, or peers. You can be acclaimed for a single work (an acclaimed debut novel), whereas renowned implies a broader, more established reputation built over time.

Illustrious means having a long and impressive history of achievement — it suggests a legacy. It is slightly more elevated and formal than renowned, and often implies a kind of glorious track record.

Reputable means having a good, trustworthy reputation, but it is much softer in intensity. A reputable plumber is reliable and honest. A renowned plumber is one that people travel miles to hire because they are considered the very best.

So while all these words share the idea of positive recognition, renowned strikes a balance — it is strong and prestigious, broader than eminent or distinguished, more enduring than acclaimed, and more respectful than merely famous.

To sharpen your understanding further:

It is not the same as popular. Popularity is about how many people like something. Renowned is about how deeply something is respected. A pop song might be enormously popular; a symphony might be renowned.

It is not notorious or infamous, which both describe recognition for something negative or disgraceful.

It is not used casually for minor or local recognition. Calling a neighborhood shopkeeper "renowned" would sound exaggerated and out of place. The word demands a level of achievement that is genuinely impressive and widely acknowledged.
Who or What Can Be Renowned?

The word can describe:

People — scientists, artists, chefs, athletes, doctors, writers, lawyers, leaders.
Places — cities, universities, hospitals, restaurants, landmarks.
Things or works — a technique, a dish, a method, an institution, a tradition.

Renowned means being widely recognized and deeply admired by many people — not simply for being well-known, but because of proven, outstanding excellence in a specific area, resulting in a lasting reputation of high prestige and respect.
13204: "Rent" as a noun has two completely separate meanings. Most people only know the first one, but a thorough understanding requires knowing both.
Meaning 1 — A regular payment for using something that belongs to someone else

This is by far the most common meaning, and the one you will encounter almost every day.

When you use something — a house, an apartment, a shop, a piece of land, a car, machinery, or any other asset — that belongs to another person, and you pay them money at regular intervals (usually monthly) in exchange for that use, that payment is called rent.

The core idea to hold onto is this: you are not buying the thing. You are paying for the temporary right to use it. Ownership never transfers to you. The thing still belongs to the original owner. When you stop paying and leave, the thing returns to the owner exactly as it was.

The person who pays rent is called a tenant (sometimes also called a renter or lessee). The person who receives rent is called a landlord (sometimes also called a lessor or property owner).

Some everyday examples:

"My rent is $1,200 a month." — This person pays $1,200 every month to live in a home they don't own.

"The landlord raised the rent." — The owner of the property increased the amount the tenant must pay.

"She earns good money from the rent on her apartments." — She is a landlord who receives payments from people living in her properties.

"The rent on the office was too steep for a small startup." — The monthly cost of using the office space was too high.

People pay rent for many kinds of things: apartments, houses, rooms, office spaces, retail shops, farmland, parking spots, storage units, and even equipment or vehicles.

Key distinctions and nuances you should know:

Rent vs. buying. When you buy something, you own it permanently after a single large payment (or a mortgage). When you rent, you never own it — you only have permission to use it temporarily, and you keep paying as long as you use it. Buying gives you ownership; renting gives you temporary use.

Rent vs. lease. These two words are closely related and are often used interchangeably in everyday speech, but there is a subtle difference. A lease usually refers to a formal, legally written agreement for a fixed period of time (for example, a one-year apartment contract). Rent is the word for the actual money paid under that agreement, and it can also describe shorter or more informal arrangements. In other words: you sign a lease, but you pay rent.

"For rent." When a property or item is available for someone to rent, it is described as for rent (common in American English) or to let (common in British English). You will often see signs saying "For Rent" outside vacant apartments.

Rent-free. If you use something "rent-free," you are using it without paying any money at all. Example: "She lives in her grandmother's cottage rent-free while she saves money." This phrase often implies a lucky or unusual arrangement.

Back rent / rent arrears. If a tenant has missed payments and owes rent from previous months, that unpaid amount is called back rent or rent arrears. Example: "He owed three months of back rent before the landlord took legal action."

Rent control. In some cities, governments place legal limits on how much landlords are allowed to charge or increase rent, in order to keep housing affordable. This policy is called rent control. It is a well-known and often debated topic in urban economics and politics.

Rent in economics (a specialized but important usage)

In formal economics, "rent" carries a more technical and broader meaning. It refers to the income earned from owning a resource — especially land — that exceeds what is strictly necessary to bring that resource into use. Think of it this way: if you own a piece of land that people desperately want and will pay a fortune for, the extra profit you make simply because you own it (not because of any work or effort you put in) is called economic rent. The land itself gives you that income just by existing.

This idea gave rise to the phrase rent-seeking, which describes behavior where a person or company tries to gain wealth by controlling resources, lobbying for favorable rules, or exploiting existing advantages — rather than by actually creating something new and valuable. You will most often encounter these economic meanings in academic writing, economics textbooks, and political discussions.
Meaning 2 — A tear, rip, or split

This meaning is completely unrelated to money. A "rent" can also mean a tear, rip, or violent split — usually in a piece of fabric or cloth, but sometimes used more broadly for cracks or gaps in other things.

This comes from the old verb to rend, which means to tear something apart forcefully. Think of it as the noun form of that violent tearing.

Examples:

"There was a large rent in his coat." — His coat had a big tear or rip in it.

"The earthquake left a deep rent in the earth." — The earthquake caused a long crack or gap in the ground.

"A rent in the storm clouds let a shaft of sunlight through." — A gap or break in the clouds allowed light to pass.

This meaning is rarely used in casual, everyday conversation today, but you will encounter it frequently in literature, poetry, and formal or old-fashioned writing. Knowing it will prevent confusion when you come across it in a book or article.
How to tell the two meanings apart

Context makes it almost effortless:

If the surrounding words involve property, housing, money, payments, landlords, or tenants — it means a regular payment for use.

If the surrounding words involve cloth, fabric, physical objects, the earth, or anything that can be physically torn — it means a tear or rip.

The two meanings are so different in their contexts that you will rarely, if ever, be genuinely confused about which one is meant.
13205: Here is the crucial thing to know upfront: "rent" as a verb actually has two completely separate meanings that have nothing to do with each other. They just happen to be spelled the same way. A thorough understanding of this word means understanding both.
Meaning 1: To Pay (or Receive) Money for Temporary Use of Something

This is by far the most common meaning in everyday modern English.

When you rent something, you pay money to use something that belongs to someone else — for a limited time. You don't own it. You use it, and as long as you keep paying, you can keep using it. When you stop paying, you give it back (or leave it).

"I rent an apartment."
This means: I pay money every month to live in an apartment. The apartment belongs to the landlord, not to me. I have the right to live there only because I keep paying.

"She rents a car when she travels."
This means: She pays a car company to use one of their cars for a short period. She returns the car when she's done.

"He rents out the spare room in his house."
This means: He lets someone else live in his spare room, and that person pays him money for it.

Notice something important in that last example: "rent" works in both directions.

  • If you are the one paying → you are renting from someone. You are the renter (also called a tenant or lessee).
  • If you are the one receiving the money → you are renting out to someone. You are the landlord (also called a lessor).

Both sides use the same verb. Context tells you which side of the deal is being described.

More examples across both directions:

"I rent my office space from a property company." → I am the one paying.
"The property company rents office space to dozens of businesses." → They are the ones receiving payment.
"Can we rent a boat for the afternoon?" → Can we pay to use a boat temporarily?
"The studio rents out its equipment to filmmakers." → The studio allows filmmakers to use its equipment for money.

A key idea that makes "rent" different from similar words:

To buy something means ownership passes to you permanently. To rent something means you never own it — you just get the right to use it for as long as you pay.

To borrow something means you use it temporarily for free. To rent it means you pay for that temporary use.

To lease something is very similar to renting, and the words are often used interchangeably in everyday speech. However, in formal or legal contexts, a lease usually refers to a longer-term, written agreement (like renting an apartment for a full year with a signed contract), whereas rent can apply to any duration, even a few hours.

The different grammatical forms of this verb:

Present: "I rent," "She rents," "They rent."
Past: "I rented," "She rented." (Regular verb — just add -ed.)
Present continuous: "I am renting an apartment downtown."
Noun form: "The rent is due on the first of each month." (Here "rent" becomes a noun meaning the money paid.)
"Rental" is a related word used as a noun ("a vacation rental") or adjective ("a rental car").
Meaning 2: The Past Tense of the Verb "Rend" (To Tear Violently)

There is an older, separate English verb — "rend" — which means to tear something apart, especially with force, violence, or raw emotion. Its past tense is not "rended." It is simply "rent."

This meaning is not commonly used in casual, everyday conversation today. But you will encounter it regularly in literature, poetry, the Bible, religious texts, and any kind of dramatic or formal writing. It is important to recognize it so that when you do encounter it, you are not confused.

"She rent her garments in grief."
This means: She tore her clothes apart out of intense sorrow. (Tearing one's clothing was historically a sign of deep mourning.)

"A tremendous crack rent the silence of the night."
This means: A loud crack violently tore through — or broke apart — the silence.

"The explosion rent the building in two."
This means: The explosion tore the building apart into two pieces.

"A cry rent the air."
This means: A cry suddenly and forcefully pierced through the air. The air, metaphorically, is being "torn" by the sound.

The core idea of "rend" (and thus "rent" in this sense) is forceful, violent tearing or splitting — whether literal (tearing cloth, splitting rock) or figurative (a sound splitting the silence, grief splitting the heart). It often carries an emotional weight and a sense of raw, uncontrolled force.

Grammatical forms of "rend":

Present: "rend" — "Strong winds rend the sails."
Past tense: "rent" — "The lightning rent the sky."
Past participle: also "rent" — "The country was rent apart by civil war."
Present participle: "rending" — "a rending, howling storm."
How to Tell the Two Meanings Apart

When you see or hear "rent" as a verb, ask yourself: is this about money and temporary use, or is it about tearing and violent force?

"I rent a house" → money and use. Meaning 1.
"The explosion rent the building apart" → tearing and force. Meaning 2 (past tense of rend).

In most everyday, modern contexts, you will encounter Meaning 1. Meaning 2 appears almost exclusively in literary, poetic, religious, or dramatic writing — and it will always be in a past-tense context describing something being torn, split, or broken apart.

"Rent" as a verb means either (1) to pay money for temporary use of something you don't own, or to receive such money for something you do own — or (2) the past tense of "rend," meaning something was violently torn apart. The first meaning is the living, everyday one. The second is literary and historical, but still very much alive on the page.
13206:
Renunciation is the deliberate, formal act of giving something up — permanently, and usually with a clear declaration. It's not simply walking away from something. It's consciously choosing to let go of something you had a right to, a claim over, or a deep attachment to, and making that choice known.

Think of the difference between quietly stopping something and formally declaring that you are done with it. Renunciation is the latter — and what you're giving up is always something of genuine value: a right, a privilege, a title, a desire, or a way of life. That's what gives the word its weight.

The verb form is renounce (you renounce something). The act of doing so is the renunciation.
The Three Worlds Where This Word Lives

Renunciation appears most powerfully in three areas of life: the legal world, the political world, and the spiritual/philosophical world.

In legal contexts, renunciation means officially surrendering a right, a status, or a legal entitlement. A person can submit a renunciation of citizenship, which is a formal legal process of giving up their nationality in a country. When someone dies and leaves you an inheritance, you can file a renunciation of inheritance, officially refusing what was left to you — people do this for tax reasons or to redirect the inheritance to someone else. An appointed executor of a will can file a renunciation of their duties, stepping away from the role. In all these cases, renunciation is never informal. It involves official declarations and real legal consequences.

In political contexts, renunciation refers to giving up power, a throne, a title, or a territorial claim — often in a public or treaty-based statement. A country might issue a renunciation of its territorial claims over a disputed region, officially declaring it will no longer pursue that land. A political movement might announce a renunciation of violence, committing to peaceful methods. These acts are significant because they involve things that affect many people and often cannot easily be undone.

In spiritual and philosophical contexts, renunciation takes on its deepest and most profound meaning. Here it refers to voluntarily giving up worldly desires, possessions, comforts, or attachments — not out of necessity, but out of a conscious pursuit of something higher. This is a central idea in Buddhism, Hinduism, Christianity, and many other traditions. A Buddhist monk practices renunciation of worldly desires, letting go of attachment to pleasure, status, and possessions in pursuit of enlightenment. In Hinduism, the final stage of life — sannyasa — is one of complete renunciation, where a person gives up all worldly ties for spiritual pursuit. A person who gives up wealth and comfort to serve the poor is living a life of material renunciation.

Crucially, in the spiritual sense, renunciation is not seen as a loss. It is seen as a liberation — you give up small things to gain something far greater: peace, freedom from suffering, or closeness to truth.

Renunciation is not a neutral word. It carries moral seriousness. A few things are always true when this word applies:

It is deliberate — never accidental. You renounce something with full awareness.

It is final — renunciation is meant to be permanent. It is not "I'm taking a break from this." It is "I am done with this."

It involves sacrifice — what is given up must have real value: a right, a privilege, a pleasure, a belief. This is precisely why renunciation earns respect or carries significance. Nobody calls it a renunciation if a child decides they don't want a toy anymore. But if a monarch gives up a crown, a billionaire gives up their wealth on principle, or a monk gives up all worldly life — that is renunciation.

It implies conviction — because you are giving up something real and valuable, the act suggests that the person doing it has strong beliefs, deep values, or serious spiritual purpose. This is why the word is often used admiringly.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Several words are close in meaning but don't quite say the same thing.

Abandonment means walking away from something — often without declaring it, and often irresponsibly. A person who abandons their family is not renouncing them; they are simply leaving. Renunciation carries dignity; abandonment often carries shame.

Rejection means refusing to accept something being offered to you. Renunciation is about giving up something you already had or were entitled to. You reject an offer; you renounce a right you already possess.

Waiver is a legal term for giving up a specific right, usually narrower and more technical in scope. All waivers involve giving something up, but not all renunciations are waivers.

Abdication specifically refers to a monarch giving up the throne. Renunciation is broader and can apply across many areas of life.

Surrender means giving up, but typically under pressure, defeat, or force. Renunciation is always voluntary — it is chosen freely, not compelled. This distinction is essential.

Disclaimer means denying responsibility for or connection to something. It's about distancing yourself, not giving up something of value.

The thread that makes renunciation unique is this: it is always voluntary, conscious, significant, and usually declared. It has a moral seriousness and a formal quality that most similar words lack.

Here are natural ways this word is used, so you can feel how it works in context:

"His renunciation of violence marked a turning point in the peace process."

"She signed the renunciation of her inheritance so her younger brother would receive the full estate."

"The monk's life was one of complete renunciation — no possessions, no attachments, no desires."

"The treaty included a formal renunciation of all territorial claims in the disputed region."

"Her renunciation of fame surprised everyone who had watched her spend years working to achieve it."

If you had to hold this word in a single thought: renunciation is the act of formally and deliberately giving up something valuable — a right, a power, a pleasure, or a way of life — as a conscious, permanent choice. It is always intentional, always significant, and almost always carries a sense of moral or personal weight.
13207:
Reparable means able to be fixed, corrected, or made right.

When something is reparable, it means the damage, mistake, or harm it caused is not permanent. There is a way back. Recovery is possible.

Think of it this way: if you accidentally scratch a wooden table, that scratch is reparable — a skilled carpenter can sand and refinish it and restore the table to its original state. But if you burn the table to ash, that is not reparable. It is gone forever.

This word is flexible. It can describe many different kinds of things:

Physical damage. A cracked wall, a broken machine, a torn garment — if these can be restored, they are reparable.

Mistakes and errors. If you send the wrong report to your boss and you can correct it before any real harm is done, that error is reparable. The situation can be recovered from.

Relationships. If two friends have an argument, their friendship might still be reparable — meaning it can be healed through conversation and effort.

Losses. In law, business, or everyday life, a loss is reparable when it can be compensated for, restored, or made up in some way.

The common thread in all these cases is this: the harm has not crossed the point of no return.
The Key to Truly Understanding It: Its Opposite

Interestingly, "reparable" is one of those words that becomes clearest when you see it next to its opposite.

The opposite is irreparable (ir- meaning "not").

  • A broken leg is reparable — it heals.
  • A permanent disability caused by an accident may be irreparable — it cannot be undone.
  • A typo in a draft document is reparable — you just correct it.
  • Saying something deeply hurtful in a public speech, destroying someone's reputation permanently, may cause irreparable damage.

Here is the important observation: in everyday writing and speech, "irreparable" is actually used far more often than "reparable." This is because people tend to emphasize when something cannot be fixed — it carries more urgency and weight. But knowing "reparable" gives you a solid foundation, and understanding one word automatically strengthens your understanding of the other.
The Tone and Register of This Word

"Reparable" is a formal word. You will most often see it in:

  • Legal writing — courts frequently discuss whether harm is reparable or irreparable when deciding whether to grant emergency orders or injunctions.
  • Academic and professional writing — essays, reports, policy documents.
  • Serious literature — novels and non-fiction dealing with consequences, ethics, and difficult situations.

In casual conversation, people rarely say "reparable." Instead, they say "fixable" or "correctable." So if your friend says, "Don't worry, it's fixable," they are expressing the same idea as "It is reparable." The meaning is identical; only the formality differs.
Similar Words and How They Differ

Several words are close to "reparable" in meaning. Knowing how they differ slightly will sharpen your understanding:

Fixable — the most casual, everyday equivalent. Refers mainly to physical things or simple problems. "The bike is fixable."

Correctable — suggests that an error or mistake can be set right. "The miscalculation is correctable." It emphasizes the idea of making something accurate again.

Remediable — means capable of being remedied. It sounds more formal and is often used for problems, situations, or conditions. "The environmental damage, though severe, is remediable."

Rectifiable — means capable of being made right or put in proper order. "The contractual error was rectifiable." This is especially common in formal and legal contexts.

All of these mean roughly the same as "reparable," but they each carry slightly different flavors. "Reparable" is the most directly tied to the idea of repair — restoring something to the state it was in before the damage occurred.

Here are examples that show the word working in different contexts:

  • "The scientist reassured the team that the error in the experiment was reparable and that they could restart the trial."
  • "The judge noted that the financial harm suffered was reparable, since the money could be returned."
  • "Their friendship, though strained, was still reparable if both sides were willing to be honest."
  • "Fortunately, the water damage to the documents was reparable, and the restoration team managed to recover them."

The word "reparable" quietly carries hope inside it. To say something is reparable is to say that the story is not over yet, that what was broken can be whole again, and that the worst outcome is not inevitable. This is why its opposite — "irreparable" — feels so heavy and final. Understanding this contrast is the deepest way to truly feel the meaning of this word, not just know its definition.
13208:
Reparation means making up for a wrong that was done. It is the act — or the result of the act — of repairing harm, damage, or injustice that one person, group, or nation caused to another.

Think of it this way: if you accidentally break your neighbor's window, saying sorry is an apology. But paying to fix that window — actually doing something to correct the harm — that is a reparation.

The key idea is not just feeling bad about a wrong. It is actively doing something to fix it or compensate for it.

The word works on two levels, and understanding both is important.

1. The Act Itself

Reparation can refer to the action of making amends. For example, someone acknowledging they caused harm and then taking steps to correct it. In this sense, you would say someone "makes reparation" for what they did. This is the moral or personal use of the word.

2. The Thing Given as Compensation

Reparation can also refer to the actual payment, gesture, or compensation given to the wronged party. This could be money, land, services, or any other form of making things right. In this sense, the reparation is the concrete thing that is handed over or offered.
Singular vs. Plural: An Important Distinction

You will frequently see this word in both its singular and plural forms, and the context shifts slightly.

Reparation (singular) tends to appear in more personal, moral, or philosophical discussions — for instance, the idea of someone owing reparation for what they did.

Reparations (plural) is extremely common in historical and political discussions, where it refers to concrete payments or compensations, usually on a large scale. This is the form you will encounter most in news, history books, and public debate.
How It Is Used in Different Contexts

In Everyday Personal Life

On a personal level, reparation is about one individual making things right with another. If someone spreads a damaging lie about you and then works to correct that lie publicly and compensates you for any losses, they are making reparation to you.

In History and Politics (War Reparations)

This is one of the most well-known uses of the word. After a war, the losing nation is sometimes required to pay war reparations to the nations it harmed. The most famous historical example is after World War I, when Germany was required to pay enormous reparations to Allied countries for the destruction and suffering caused by the war. These payments were meant to compensate for economic losses, physical damage, and human suffering.

In Social Justice Discussions

The word is widely used in debates about historical injustices — such as slavery, colonialism, or ethnic persecution. In these conversations, reparations refers to the idea that governments or institutions should compensate the descendants of people who were wronged, acknowledging that past injustices continue to cause harm in the present. Whether such reparations should be paid, to whom, in what form, and how much are all deeply debated questions, but the word itself simply names the concept of that compensation.

In Law

In a legal context, reparation can refer to what a court orders a wrongdoer to give a victim. It is similar to damages — a sum of money or action required to repair the harm caused.
What Makes Reparation Different from Similar Words

These words are related but not identical:

Apology — words expressing regret. An apology alone is not a reparation.

Compensation — very close in meaning, but compensation is broader. You can be compensated for things that were nobody's fault (like an insurance payout). Reparation specifically implies a wrong was committed and is being addressed.

Restitution — this means returning something that was taken, restoring things to their original state. Reparation is wider — it doesn't just mean returning what was taken; it means making up for the harm in whatever way is appropriate, even if the original thing can't be returned.

Repair — reparation shares its root idea with repair, and you can think of them as cousins. Repair fixes a broken object; reparation "fixes" a broken moral, social, or legal relationship.
The Emotional and Moral Weight of the Word

Reparation is not a neutral word. It carries weight because it implies:

  1. A wrong was committed — someone caused harm.
  2. Responsibility is acknowledged — the wrongdoer (or their successors) accepts that harm was done.
  3. An obligation exists — something must be done about it, not just acknowledged.

This is why the word appears so often in serious moral and political conversations. It moves the discussion from "we feel bad about what happened" to "what are we actually going to do about it?"
A Simple Summary to Lock It In

Reparation is the act of making amends for a wrong, or the actual payment/compensation given to do so. It says: something bad was done, someone is responsible, and something concrete must be offered to make it right.

Whether it is one person apologizing with action to another, a defeated nation paying for wartime destruction, or a government addressing a historical injustice — the word always carries those same three elements: a wrong, responsibility, and a remedy.
13209: Repartee is the art of the quick, clever comeback — and the sparkling, witty conversation built from such comebacks flying back and forth between people.

When someone says something to you, and you instantly fire back with a sharp, intelligent, funny reply — that reply is repartee. And when a whole conversation is full of those fast, clever exchanges, the entire conversation is also called repartee. So the word works both ways: it can describe a single brilliant comeback, or an entire style of back-and-forth wit.
The Three Things That Make Something "Repartee"

For something to truly be repartee, it needs all three of these qualities at once:

1. It must be quick. Repartee is spontaneous — it comes right away, in the moment. If you sit and think for five minutes before saying something witty, it's no longer repartee, because the moment has passed.

2. It must be witty. It's not just funny — it's clever. Repartee has intelligence behind it. It's sharp and polished, not silly or accidental.

3. It must be a reply. This is crucial. Repartee doesn't happen in a vacuum. It is always a response to something someone else said. It reacts, bounces off what was said, and turns it around brilliantly. A random joke you tell out of nowhere is not repartee. A perfectly aimed comeback that responds to exactly what the other person just said — that's repartee.

It helps to draw a clear line:

  • A joke you prepared and memorized → not repartee (it wasn't spontaneous)
  • A slow, thoughtful response → not repartee (it wasn't quick)
  • A funny random observation → not repartee (it wasn't a reply to anything)
  • Ordinary casual small talk → not repartee (it isn't witty or sharp)
A Simple Example to Feel It

Imagine someone at a party looks at you and says, mockingly: "You look exhausted — like you haven't slept in three days."

Scenario A: You pause, think for a minute, scratch your head, and eventually say something funny. → Not repartee. Too slow.

Scenario B: Without missing a beat, you shoot back: "I couldn't sleep — I kept thinking about how worried I am for your haircut." The room laughs. → That's repartee. It was instant, it was witty, and it directly responded to what they said.

One of the most celebrated examples of repartee in history is a short exchange between Winston Churchill and Lady Astor. She said to him: "If you were my husband, I would put poison in your coffee." Without hesitation, Churchill replied: "If you were my wife, I would drink it."

That is repartee in its purest form — lightning fast, devastatingly clever, and completely shaped by what the other person just said.
Think of It as Verbal Tennis

Picture a tennis match — but instead of hitting balls, the players are hitting witty remarks. Each player returns the shot faster, sharper, and more brilliantly than the last. The whole match, with both players exchanging these quick, dazzling shots, is repartee. Each individual brilliant shot is also repartee.

The key is that the ball is always moving. There's no pause, no hesitation — just swift, sharp, elegant play.

The word is also used to describe a person's ability to do this — their talent for always having the perfect witty reply ready in an instant.

  • "She is famous for her repartee" → she has a gift for quick, clever comebacks
  • "He lacks repartee" → he struggles to think of the right thing to say in the moment
  • "The two comedians dazzled the audience with their repartee" → their witty back-and-forth was the highlight

This is why repartee is deeply admired. It requires a fast mind, a sharp sense of humor, confidence, and a natural way with language — all firing at the same time, instantly.

Repartee is playful by nature, but it often carries a cutting edge — like a velvet glove with a sword inside. It can be warm and funny between friends, or sharp and pointed between rivals. Either way, when done well, it tends to make everyone in the room smile, even when the remarks are barbed. It's never clumsy, never slow, never accidental. It's effortless-looking — which is exactly what makes it so impressive.

In short: repartee is the gold standard of conversational wit — the ability to respond to what someone says with something so clever, so fast, and so perfectly aimed that people are still thinking about it long after the conversation ends.
13210:
A repast simply means a meal — the food and drink you consume at one sitting. That's it. It can be breakfast, lunch, dinner, or any other eating occasion, large or small.

But what makes this word special is the flavor it carries. "Repast" is a formal, literary word. You'll find it in novels, poetry, and old stories — rarely in everyday conversation. When a writer chooses "repast" over "meal," they're giving the act of eating a sense of dignity and ceremony, almost as if the meal deserves to be appreciated and remembered.

Compare:

  • "We ate a meal." → Plain. Neutral. Nothing special.
  • "We sat down to a repast." → Elevated. Ceremonious. Almost elegant.
It can describe any kind of meal

A repast doesn't have to be grand. It can be humble or magnificent — writers just use adjectives to show which:

  • a simple repast — a plain, modest meal
  • a light repast — just a small bite, something easy
  • a frugal repast — bare minimum, barely enough
  • a sumptuous repast — rich, lavish, and impressive

• "After the long journey, the travelers were grateful for a warm repast of stew and bread."
  • "The family gathered for a quiet repast following the funeral."
  • "He called it a midnight snack, but it was really a full repast — roast chicken, potatoes, and wine."

You'll mostly see "repast" in:

  • Classic or 19th-century fiction
  • Poetry and formal writing
  • Sometimes in modern writing as gentle irony — calling a bag of crackers "an evening repast" is a joke, playing on how fancy the word sounds

In casual, everyday speech, "repast" sounds stiff and old-fashioned. Telling a friend "I'm heading home for my repast" will likely get a puzzled look. Stick to "meal," "lunch," "dinner," etc. in normal conversation. Save "repast" for writing, or for deliberately elegant or humorous effect.

A repast is a formal, literary word for a meal of any kind — used when the writer wants to give eating a sense of occasion, elegance, or ceremonial weight, rather than treating it as an ordinary everyday act.
13211: To repatriate means to send someone or something back to the country it originally came from or belongs to. The key idea is always a return — back home, back to the place of origin.

Think of it this way: if you are a citizen of France but you are currently stuck, living, imprisoned, or stranded in another country, and someone arranges to send you back to France — that is repatriation. France is your patria (your homeland), and you are being sent back to it. The person or authority doing this is said to repatriate you.

It is almost always used in formal, official, or serious contexts — government decisions, international law, diplomacy, corporate finance, and humanitarian affairs. You would rarely hear it in casual conversation.
The Three Main Things That Get Repatriated

The word applies to three broad categories:

1. People

This is the most common use. A government, international body, or organization repatriates a person when it arranges for them to be returned to their home country. This happens in many situations:

  • Citizens who are stranded, evacuated, or rescued abroad are repatriated by their own government. For example, when a war breaks out in a foreign country, embassies often work urgently to repatriate their nationals.
  • Prisoners of war are repatriated to their home countries after a conflict ends.
  • Refugees or migrants are sometimes repatriated — returned to their country of origin — either voluntarily or by force.
  • The remains (the body) of a person who died in a foreign country are repatriated — sent back home for burial.

2. Money and Assets

Companies and individuals can also repatriate money. When a multinational company earns profits in a foreign country and transfers that money back to its home country, it is said to repatriate those profits. For example: "Apple decided to repatriate billions of dollars it had held in overseas accounts." The money is being "returned" to the country where the company is headquartered.

3. Cultural Artifacts and Objects

This use has become very prominent in modern debates about museums and history. When a country demands that a historical object — a sculpture, a painting, ancient relics — be returned from a foreign museum or institution to the country it was originally taken from, that return is called repatriation. For example: "Greece has long campaigned for Britain to repatriate the Elgin Marbles." The objects are being sent back to where they rightfully originated.

An important nuance: repatriation can be either willing or unwilling. A person can voluntarily agree to be repatriated — perhaps they want to go home. Or they can be repatriated against their will, by force or by a government order. The word itself does not tell you which one it is; you need the surrounding context to understand that.

Typically, the subject of the verb — the one doing the repatriating — is an authority of some kind: a government, an international organization (like the United Nations or the Red Cross), a court, or a corporation. Regular individuals don't usually "repatriate" each other. The scale and official nature of the action is implied in the word.
How Is It Different From Similar Words?

This is crucial to get right, because a few words can seem similar but are actually different.

Repatriate vs. Deport: Deportation specifically means forcibly removing a person from a country because they violated that country's immigration laws. Repatriation is broader — it can be voluntary, humanitarian, or diplomatic, and it specifically emphasizes the return to the home country, not just removal from a country. All deportations send people away, but not all repatriations are forced, and not all deportations send people to their homeland (they go to wherever their citizenship is recognized).

Repatriate vs. Extradite: To extradite someone means to hand them over to another country specifically so they can face criminal charges or serve a sentence there. The destination is not necessarily their home country — it's the country where they allegedly committed a crime. Repatriation is not about criminal prosecution; it's about returning to one's country of origin.

Repatriate vs. Immigrate/Emigrate: These words describe someone choosing to move from one country to another for a new life. Repatriation is specifically a return — going back to where you are originally from, often under official or formal arrangements.

To cement your understanding, here are clear, varied examples:

  • "The airline worked with the embassy to repatriate the tourists who were stranded after the earthquake."
  • "After years of lobbying, the museum finally agreed to repatriate the stolen artifacts to Nigeria."
  • "Many foreign workers chose to repatriate when the economy collapsed in their host country."
  • "The soldier's remains were repatriated with full military honors."
  • "The new tax law gave corporations a strong incentive to repatriate their offshore earnings."
  • "The refugee was repatriated despite her protests that it was not safe for her to return."

If you ever need to recall it instantly: to repatriate = to officially send someone or something back to the country they originally came from.

Everything else — whether it's a person, money, or an artifact; whether it's voluntary or forced; whether it's done out of compassion or obligation — is just the context surrounding that one clean, precise idea.
13212:
Repatriation is the act or process of returning someone or something back to the country it originally came from or belongs to.

Think of it this way: imagine you are a citizen of France, but you are stranded in another country — as a refugee, a prisoner of war, or someone caught in a foreign crisis. The process of being returned to France is called your repatriation. The same word applies when a priceless painting taken from Italy 200 years ago is returned to Italy — that is also repatriation.

The word almost always carries the idea of a "going back" to a place of origin or belonging. It is used for people, for objects, for money, and even for the bodies of people who die in foreign lands.

This is the most common use of the word. When a person is sent back to their home country, that is repatriation. It occurs in several situations.

Prisoners of war are a classic example. After a war ends, soldiers held captive in enemy territory are returned to their home countries. This is called the repatriation of prisoners of war, and it has been a formal part of peace agreements throughout modern history.

Refugees and displaced persons are another major context. People who have fled their home countries because of war, persecution, or disaster may eventually return when conditions improve. That journey back is called repatriation. It can be voluntary — meaning they choose to return — or forced, meaning they are made to go back against their will.

Stranded citizens abroad are also repatriated. When a government organizes emergency flights or ships to bring its citizens home from a foreign crisis — a war zone, a natural disaster, or a global emergency — that whole operation is called a repatriation effort.

Undocumented migrants whose presence in a country is not legally permitted may be returned to their home country by the authorities. This too is called repatriation, though it overlaps with deportation in some contexts (a distinction explained below).
When It Refers to Human Remains

When a person dies in a foreign country, their body is often returned to their home country for burial or cremation according to the family's wishes. This process is called the repatriation of remains, and it involves legal paperwork, coordination between governments, and careful transport. For grieving families, it is often a deeply emotional and important process.
When It Refers to Cultural Property

This is one of the most discussed and debated uses of the word in the modern world. Over the centuries — especially during the era of colonialism — many countries took valuable artifacts, sculptures, paintings, manuscripts, and sacred objects from other nations. Today, a large number of these items sit in museums in Europe and North America, far from the places they came from.

When such items are returned to their countries of origin, that act is called cultural repatriation or the repatriation of cultural property.

For example, if Nigeria formally requests that a British museum return bronze sculptures taken from the Kingdom of Benin in the 1800s, and those sculptures are handed back, their return is called repatriation. This is a major ongoing conversation in international relations, museum ethics, and questions of justice and history.

Repatriation also has an important financial meaning. When a company or a person earns money in a foreign country and brings that money back to their home country, that process is called the repatriation of funds, or profit repatriation, or capital repatriation.

For example, a large multinational company that operates in dozens of countries around the world may accumulate profits in those countries. When it transfers that money back to its headquarters country, that is repatriation of earnings. Governments sometimes design special tax policies to encourage companies to repatriate their money, so that it flows back into the domestic economy.

This distinction matters a great deal, especially when the word is used for people.

Voluntary repatriation is when someone willingly chooses to return to their home country. A refugee who decides the situation back home has improved enough to go back is voluntarily repatriating.

Forced repatriation is when someone is sent back against their will, usually by government authorities. This is often controversial and is considered a human rights concern when the person being sent back faces danger or persecution in their home country.

These two words are sometimes confused, but they are meaningfully different.

Deportation is the act of expelling someone from a country — typically because they violated a law or immigration rule. It carries a negative, legal connotation and is almost always forced. The person being deported may not necessarily be sent to their own home country; they are simply removed from the country they were in.

Repatriation is specifically about returning to one's own country or place of origin. It is used across a much wider range of contexts — for people, objects, money, and human remains. It does not carry an inherently negative connotation and can be either a voluntary or a compassionate act.

In short: all deportations involve removing someone, but not all repatriations are deportations. A refugee choosing to go home is being repatriated, not deported.

To recognize the word in the real world, here are the phrases most commonly built around it: repatriation of refugees, repatriation of remains, repatriation of cultural artifacts, repatriation of funds or capital or profits, voluntary repatriation, forced repatriation, and repatriation program or repatriation flight.
The Deeper Feeling of the Word

Repatriation carries a sense of things being returned to where they rightfully belong. Whether it is a person going home after years of displacement, a stolen sculpture being returned to the people it was made for, or earnings coming back to their country of origin, the word always suggests a journey back — a restoration of something to its proper place. It is a word that sits at the crossroads of law, history, justice, and human dignity.
13213:
To repeal something means to officially and completely cancel a law, rule, or regulation that was previously established, so that it no longer exists or has any legal effect. Think of it as "officially undoing" a law — wiping it off the books entirely.

A key thing to understand right away: repeal is a formal, authoritative act. It is not someone simply deciding to ignore a law, or a court saying a law was unfair. It is the official removal of a law by a body that has the power to do so — usually a parliament, congress, or legislature.
The Key Idea: Gone, Not Just Changed

The most important thing about "repeal" is that it means complete removal, not just modification.

When a law is repealed, it does not get weakened, adjusted, or suspended. It is gone. It ceases to exist as a law. Nobody is bound by it anymore. This is what separates "repeal" from words like "amend" (which means to change a law, while keeping it alive).

Think of it this way: if a law were a rule written on a blackboard, amending it would be erasing some words and rewriting them. Repealing it would be erasing the whole thing entirely.
Who Repeals, and What Gets Repealed?

Who repeals: Typically, the same body that created the law — a government, a parliament, a congress, or a legislature. A new government might repeal laws passed by a previous government. A legislature can repeal its own old laws.

What gets repealed: Almost always a law, act, statute, regulation, or policy — things that were formally enacted in the first place. You repeal things that were officially created through a legal or governmental process.

Common things that get repealed:

  • National laws and acts (e.g., "Congress repealed the act.")
  • Tax laws (e.g., "The government repealed the fuel tax.")
  • Bans and prohibitions (e.g., "They repealed the ban on imports.")
  • Constitutional amendments, in some cases

Understanding what a word doesn't mean is just as important as knowing what it does.

Repeal does not mean "ignore." If a government simply stops enforcing a law but doesn't formally remove it, that is not a repeal. The law still technically exists on paper.

Repeal does not apply to personal decisions. You wouldn't say "I repealed my decision to go to the gym." It is a legal/governmental term, not an everyday personal one.

Repeal does not mean "suspend." Suspending a law means putting it on pause temporarily. Repealing it means ending it permanently.

Repeal is not the same as a court striking down a law. When a court (like a Supreme Court) declares a law unconstitutional and invalid, that is usually described as "striking down" or "overturning" the law — not repealing it. Repeal specifically refers to a legislative (law-making) body removing a law, not a judicial (court) body.

These words are often confused with "repeal," but they have distinct meanings:

Amend: To change or modify a law. The law still lives, but parts of it are altered. ("They amended the contract to include a new clause.") Repeal removes the whole thing; amendment edits it.

Revoke: To cancel a specific permission, license, or privilege granted to a person or entity. ("Her driving license was revoked.") Revoke is more personal and specific; repeal is broader and legislative.

Abolish: To formally bring something to an end — often used for institutions, systems, or practices, not just laws. ("They abolished slavery.") Abolish has a wider, more sweeping feel. Repeal is specifically about cancelling a formal law or act.

Annul: To declare something void — as if it never existed or was never valid. Often used in contexts like marriage ("The marriage was annulled."). Repeal doesn't pretend the law never existed; it simply ends it going forward.

Rescind: To cancel an order, decision, or agreement, often in a business or contractual context. ("The company rescinded the job offer.") Rescind is less formal and legislative than repeal.

The cleanest summary: repeal is specifically and almost exclusively used for the legislative cancellation of a law or formal act.

Here are examples showing how "repeal" is used naturally:

  • "Parliament voted to repeal the outdated law."
  • "Activists spent years campaigning to repeal the ban."
  • "The new president promised to repeal several regulations introduced by his predecessor."
  • "The prohibition on alcohol was repealed in 1933, ending the era of Prohibition in the United States."
  • "Critics argued that repealing the environmental law would cause serious harm."
  • "Once the law was repealed, businesses were free to operate without those restrictions."

Notice that you can use repeal in different tenses: repeal, repeals, repealed, repealing.
A Real-World Example to Make It Stick

One of the most famous real-world examples of repeal is the 18th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, which introduced Prohibition — making it illegal to produce or sell alcohol. It was later repealed by the 21st Amendment in 1933, which cancelled the ban entirely and made alcohol legal again.

This example shows the essence of the word perfectly: a law that existed was formally, officially, and completely removed by the appropriate authority, so it no longer had any force.

If you had to carry just one definition in your head:

To repeal means to officially and permanently cancel a law or formal rule, so that it no longer has any legal effect.
13214: Repel means to push something away, or to force something to stay away. Think of it as the exact opposite of attract. Where attract pulls things closer, repel drives them apart or keeps them at a distance. This pushing away can happen in three distinct ways — physically, emotionally, and practically/materially.
Sense 1 — To push back or drive away by force

This is the most literal meaning. When a force pushes something away, or when a person or group actively drives something back, we say they repel it.

The clearest example in nature is magnets. Hold two magnets with the same poles facing each other, and they push each other away — they repel each other. No matter how hard you try, an invisible force keeps them apart.

In a military context, if an army successfully fights off an enemy attack and forces the attackers to retreat, they have repelled the attack. The key idea is that something was coming and it was driven back.

"The soldiers repelled the enemy's advance."
"The two poles of the magnets repelled each other."
Sense 2 — To cause strong disgust or aversion in someone

This is the most common everyday use, and it's important to understand how strong this feeling is. To be repelled by something is not just to dislike it quietly — it is to feel such strong disgust that you experience an almost physical urge to turn away, move away, or get as far from it as possible. It is a powerful, instinctive reaction.

A smell, a sight, a behavior, or a person's attitude can all repel someone. The subject doing the repelling is the thing causing the disgust, and the object is the person being affected.

"The sight of the infected wound repelled him completely."
"Her cruelty repelled everyone who met her."
"I was repelled by the way he treated the staff."

Notice that last example: you can say either "It repelled me" or "I was repelled by it" — both are grammatically correct and mean the same thing.

An important nuance here: being repelled is involuntary. You don't decide to feel repelled; the feeling comes to you as a natural reaction, almost like a reflex. This is what separates repel from simply dislike. You might dislike a bland meal and quietly push the plate away. But a plate of maggots would repel you — you'd feel a gut-level, urgent need to look away or leave. The word carries that intensity.
Sense 3 — To resist or block something from passing through

Some materials or substances are designed to prevent something from entering, penetrating, or coming near. When they successfully do this, we say they repel that thing.

"This jacket repels water." (Water cannot soak in; it runs right off the surface.)
"The spray repels mosquitoes." (Mosquitoes are driven away and kept from coming near.)
"The coating on the pan repels grease."

This is the exact reason we call insect-repelling products repellents — they repel (keep away) insects. The word "repellent" comes directly from this use.

Repel is always a transitive verb, which means it always needs an object. It must repel something or someone. You cannot use it without specifying what is being pushed away.

✅ "The smell repelled the guests."
❌ "The smell repelled." ← This is incomplete. Repelled whom? Repelled what?

The antonym of repel is attract — to pull something toward you, or to make someone feel drawn in. These two words are perfect mirrors of each other:

  • A magnet can either attract iron filings or repel them.
  • A person's warmth might attract others; their arrogance might repel them.
  • A bright light attracts moths, but certain chemicals repel them.

Understanding this pair helps anchor the meaning of repel firmly in your mind.

Repellent (adjective) — describes something that repels in the emotional sense. "A repellent personality" means a personality so off-putting that people instinctively want to stay away.

Repellent (noun) — a substance designed to keep something away. "Insect repellent," "mosquito repellent," "tick repellent."

Repulsive (adjective) — very similar to repellent in the emotional sense, but often even stronger. If something is repulsive, it causes a deep, almost nauseating disgust. "The scene was repulsive." You can think of repellent and repulsive as near-synonyms in everyday use, with repulsive being the more intense of the two.

Repulsion (noun) — the feeling or force of being repelled. "She felt a wave of repulsion when she heard his words." In physics, it also refers to the force by which like charges or magnetic poles push each other apart.

The single thread connecting all three senses of repel is this: something is being pushed away, or kept away. Whether it's an army being driven back, a person being disgusted into moving away, or water being blocked from soaking through a surface — the core idea is always the same. Repel is a word about distance, separation, and resistance. Wherever you see it, ask yourself: what is being pushed away, and by what? The answer will always make the meaning clear.
13215:
To repent means to feel deep, genuine sorrow for something wrong that you have done — and to sincerely wish you had not done it — while also having a strong desire to change your ways and not repeat that wrong.

Notice that definition has three parts. All three matter:

  1. You feel deep sorrow (not just mild embarrassment)
  2. You recognize what you did was genuinely wrong
  3. You have a desire to change — to do better going forward

This is important because repentance is never just a feeling you sit with. It always points forward. A person who repents is not just crying about the past; they are making an inner commitment to be different.
The One Thing That Makes "Repent" Unique

Many words describe feeling bad about something. What makes repent stand out is the combination of moral guilt + inner transformation.

Think of it this way:

  • You can regret eating too much cake. → That's just disappointment in an outcome.
  • You can regret a car accident you didn't cause. → That's sadness, not guilt.
  • But you repent when you did something morally wrong, you know it was wrong, and you genuinely want to become the kind of person who would not do it again.

Repentance is always personal, always moral, and always involves a turning of the heart.

In a religious context

This is where the word is most at home, and where its full weight is felt. In religions like Christianity, Islam, and Judaism, to repent means to turn away from sin — to stand before God (or your conscience) and say: "I did wrong. I am sorry. I will not go back to that." It is considered a serious, sacred act, not a casual one.

"The preacher called on his congregation to repent and seek forgiveness."

In everyday, secular use

Outside of religion, the word is used more broadly but carries the same emotional seriousness. It means to deeply regret a wrong decision or harmful action — one that hurt others or violated your own values.

"Years later, he repented the way he had treated his old friend."
"She repented her dishonesty the moment she saw the hurt on his face."

In secular use, "repent" is slightly formal or literary in tone. In casual conversation, people more often say "I deeply regret" or "I'm so sorry for what I did." But when a writer or speaker uses repent in a non-religious context, they are deliberately signaling a deeper, more profound kind of remorse — one that touches the person's character, not just their actions.
How to Use It in a Sentence

The verb repent can be used in several patterns:

1. Repent + of + something
This is the most traditional and common pattern.

"He repented of his greed."
"She repented of every cruel word she had ever spoken."

2. Repent + for + something
Very similar in meaning, and widely accepted.

"He repented for his past mistakes."

3. Repent + something (direct object, no preposition)
Used more in literary or religious writing.

"He repented his betrayal."

4. Repent alone (no object)
The speaker doesn't name a specific wrong — just the act of repenting itself.

"It is never too late to repent."
"He lived a selfish life and refused to repent."

Repent vs. Regret
Regret is wider and softer. You can regret things that were not your fault, were not morally wrong, or were simply unfortunate choices. Repent is narrower and deeper — it is always about something morally wrong that you did.
