Almost anything — a person, a behavior, an idea, a smell, a policy, a practice, a system. However, in practice, it is most often used to describe:

  • Human behavior or actions — cruelty, exploitation, betrayal, violence
  • Ideas or ideologies — racism, oppression, injustice
  • Policies or laws — especially those seen as violating human rights or dignity
  • Physical things — foul smells, rotting objects, disgusting sights

"The practice of slavery is repugnant to any civilized conscience."
"He found the politician's dishonesty repugnant."
"The smell of the decaying fish was repugnant."
What Makes "Repugnant" Different from Similar Words?

There are several words that seem similar. Here is how "repugnant" stands apart:

Disgusting — focuses on the gut-level reaction of revulsion. It can be used casually and for trivial things ("This pizza is disgusting"). Repugnant is weightier and almost always implies a moral dimension.

Offensive — means something causes hurt or insult. It is softer than repugnant. You can be mildly offensive. You cannot be mildly repugnant.

Abhorrent — very close in meaning to repugnant, and equally strong. The slight difference is that abhorrent emphasizes hatred and detestation, while repugnant emphasizes the sense of something being fundamentally wrong and offensive to your values or senses.

Revolting — primarily a physical, sensory reaction (something that makes you want to turn away). Repugnant is broader and carries more moral weight.

Loathsome — means deeply hateful, often with contempt mixed in. Repugnant focuses more on the wrongness of something than on hatred toward it.

The best way to lock this word in your memory is to think of the feeling, not just the definition.

Imagine you witness something deeply cruel, or you read about a monstrous injustice, and you feel a wave of disgust rise inside you — a feeling that says this violates something fundamental in me, in society, in humanity. That feeling, and the thing that caused it, is what "repugnant" describes.

It is the word you reach for when something does not just bother you, but when it conflicts with your deepest sense of what is right, decent, and human.

What it meansDeeply, strongly disgusting or morally offensive; or (formally) in direct conflict with something
How strongVery strong — near the top of the scale of displeasure
Used forBehaviors, ideas, policies, smells, practices — anything deeply offensive
ToneSerious, formal, morally charged
Key phrase"repugnant to" — meaning offensive to, or incompatible with

"Cruelty in any form is repugnant to a compassionate society."

That one sentence captures the word perfectly.
13247: Repulse means to push something or someone away — but depending on the context, that "pushing away" can happen in three very different ways: physically, socially, or emotionally. Think of it as one word with three layers of meaning, all connected by the same idea of rejection and force.
Meaning 1: To Fight Off and Push Back (Physical / Military)

This is the oldest and most literal meaning. When an army, a group, or a person repulses an attack or an attacker, they successfully resist and drive them back by force.

The key idea here is not just blocking, but actively pushing the threat away.

Examples:

  • "The soldiers repulsed the enemy's charge and held the fort."
  • "The goalkeeper repulsed every attempt to score."
  • "The city repulsed three invasions before finally falling."

Think of it this way: if someone tries to knock down your door and you not only stop them but force them back into the street — you have repulsed them.
Meaning 2: To Coldly Reject or Rebuff (Social)

In a social or personal situation, to repulse someone means to firmly and often coldly turn them away — to refuse their request, their affection, or their attempt to get close to you.

This isn't a gentle "no, thank you." It carries a sense of deliberate, and sometimes harsh, rejection.

Examples:

  • "He tried to make conversation with her, but she repulsed him with a sharp glare."
  • "Every time he offered help, she repulsed him."
  • "The celebrity repulsed all attempts by the journalist to get an interview."

The person being repulsed here is left feeling shut out, rejected, and possibly embarrassed.
Meaning 3: To Cause Disgust or Strong Revulsion (Emotional / Sensory)

This is the most commonly used sense in modern, everyday English. When something repulses you, it causes you to feel intense disgust or revulsion — a powerful, almost physical reaction of "get this away from me."

Examples:

  • "The rotting smell from the bin repulsed her the moment she walked in."
  • "He was repulsed by the cruelty he witnessed."
  • "The graphic images repulsed the entire audience."

Notice that in this meaning, the subject (the thing doing the repulsing) is usually the cause of disgust — a smell, a sight, a behavior — and the object (the person being repulsed) is the one experiencing it.

All three meanings share the same invisible thread — forceful rejection:

  • In Meaning 1, it is a physical force that pushes something back.
  • In Meaning 2, it is a social force that pushes a person away.
  • In Meaning 3, it is an emotional/sensory force that makes you want to retreat from something.

You can think of repulse as the word you use when rejection isn't mild or neutral — it always involves some kind of strong, active pushing away, whether on a battlefield, in a conversation, or in your gut.

Repulse is a transitive verb, meaning it always needs an object — something or someone being repulsed. It cannot stand alone.

The most common patterns are:

  • [Someone] repulsed [an attack / an attacker] → Meaning 1
  • [Someone] repulsed [a person] → Meaning 2
  • [Something] repulsed [someone] → Meaning 3

Notice how Meaning 3 flips the typical sentence structure — the thing causing disgust is the subject, and the person feeling disgust is the object. This is similar to how the verbs "disgust," "horrify," and "nauseate" work.

You can also use it in the passive voice:

  • "She was repulsed by his behavior." (= His behavior repulsed her.)
  • "The attack was repulsed within hours."

Repulse vs. Repel:
These two are very close siblings. In fact, they are interchangeable in most situations. However, repel is more common in everyday speech, while repulse tends to feel slightly more formal, dramatic, or literary. If you're writing a novel about a battle or a deeply unpleasant experience, "repulse" carries more weight. In casual conversation, "repel" sounds more natural.

Repulse vs. Disgust:
"Disgust" is purely about the feeling of revulsion. "Repulse" carries that same emotional meaning but adds a layer of force — it doesn't just make you feel sick, it makes you want to actively turn away or retreat. "Repulse" is stronger and more visceral.

Repulse vs. Reject:
"Reject" is neutral and common. It simply means to say no to something. "Repulse," in its social meaning, implies a harsher, more cutting form of rejection — one that leaves the other person feeling pushed away, not just declined.

Repulse vs. Rebuff:
These are very similar in the social meaning. Both describe a sharp rejection. The difference is subtle: rebuff is almost always about rejecting a person's friendly or romantic approach, while repulse in the social sense can apply more broadly to any kind of advance, request, or effort.

The adjective repulsive describes something that causes disgust — "a repulsive smell," "repulsive behavior."

The past participle repulsed describes how a person feels after experiencing that disgust — "I was repulsed by the smell."

Both come from the same verb, but they describe different sides of the experience: the cause versus the reaction.

MeaningContextThe force involved
  • Push back physically → Used in battles, sports, and physical confrontations.
  • Reject someone socially → Used when someone is turned away coldly and firmly.
  • Cause disgust → Used when something triggers a powerful, gut-level aversion.

In all three cases, "repulse" is never a soft word. It always describes something forceful, sharp, and unambiguous. When something or someone is repulsed, there is no question about it — the rejection is complete.
13248:
If something is repulsive, it causes a strong, almost physical feeling of disgust, revulsion, or extreme dislike — the kind of reaction that makes you want to turn away, back away, or escape from it entirely. It is not merely unpleasant. It is so deeply offensive to your senses or your sense of decency that your gut instinct is to reject it completely.

Think of it this way: when you encounter something repulsive, your whole body seems to react — you might wince, shudder, feel your stomach turn, or feel an urgent desire to get away. The reaction is involuntary and powerful.

"Repulsive" has two distinct meanings — one used in everyday life, and one used in science.

1. The Everyday Meaning (Far More Common)

This is the meaning you will encounter almost everywhere. Something repulsive produces an intense feeling of disgust or loathing. It deeply offends your senses — sight, smell, taste, hearing — or your moral sense of what is decent and acceptable.

Examples in sentences:

  • "The wound had a repulsive smell that made everyone step back."
  • "His cruel treatment of animals was repulsive to all who witnessed it."
  • "She found the idea of eating raw meat repulsive."
  • "The villain in the story was not just evil — he was utterly repulsive in his arrogance and cruelty."

Notice how in each case, the reaction is not mild. It is a full, strong rejection — emotional or physical or both.

2. The Scientific Meaning (Physics)

In physics, "repulsive" describes a force that pushes things apart. When two magnets face each other at the same poles (north-north or south-south), they push each other away. That pushing force is called a repulsive force. The same idea applies to electric charges — two like charges repel each other, so the force between them is repulsive.

Example: "The repulsive force between the two positively charged particles prevented them from touching."

This scientific meaning is actually the origin of the everyday meaning — both share the same root idea of pushing away. Something repulsive in everyday life pushes you away emotionally, just as a repulsive force pushes objects away physically.
What Can Be Described as Repulsive?

"Repulsive" is a very flexible adjective. It can describe:

A person's appearance — "The creature in the horror film had a repulsive, rotting face."

A smell or taste — "The repulsive stench of the swamp made it impossible to breathe normally."

A behavior or action — "Lying to a grieving widow for personal gain is repulsive."

An idea or attitude — "Many people find extreme hate speech repulsive."

A personality or character — "Despite his wealth, his selfishness made him repulsive as a person."

The common thread in all these uses is the same: a strong, instinctive feeling of "I cannot stand this. I need to get away from it."

"Repulsive" sits near the extreme end of the scale of negativity. To understand where it sits, consider this rough scale of intensity for describing something unpleasant:

Mildly unpleasant → Unpleasant → Disagreeable → Distasteful → Disgusting → Repulsive

"Repulsive" is among the strongest words on this scale. When you call something repulsive, you are saying that your reaction to it is one of deep, visceral rejection — not just mild discomfort.
How Is It Different from Similar Words?

Several words are close in meaning to "repulsive," but each has a slightly different shade.

Disgusting is probably the closest synonym. The two words are nearly interchangeable. However, "repulsive" carries a slightly stronger sense of wanting to physically pull away, while "disgusting" leans more toward moral or sensory outrage. In practice, most native speakers use them interchangeably.

Revolting is also very similar — perhaps equally strong. "The food was revolting" and "The food was repulsive" mean essentially the same thing.

Offensive is broader and milder. Something offensive might hurt your feelings, disrespect you, or cross a social boundary — but it doesn't necessarily make your stomach turn. Repulsive does.

Hideous usually refers specifically to appearance — something hideous is visually very ugly. Repulsive can refer to appearance, but it can also refer to smell, behavior, ideas, and personality.

Vile is similarly strong, but "vile" often carries a moral weight — vile acts are not just disgusting but wicked. Repulsive is more about the reaction it causes than the moral judgment itself.
Repulsive vs. Repelled — A Quick Note

The adjective "repulsive" describes the thing causing the reaction. The reaction itself — the feeling of being pushed away — is described by the verb "repel" or the adjective "repelled."

  • "The smell was repulsive." (The smell is the repulsive thing.)
  • "I was repelled by the smell." (I am the one who experienced the reaction.)

This is a small but important distinction when using the word correctly.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

When you call something repulsive, you are communicating something powerful. You are not just saying you dislike something — you are saying it provokes a strong, unwilling, near-instinctive reaction of rejection. This makes it a word with significant emotional force. Using it casually about small things (like a flavor you don't prefer) would be an exaggeration. It is best reserved for things that genuinely provoke a deep sense of disgust, revulsion, or moral outrage.

Repulsive means causing such a strong feeling of disgust or dislike that you instinctively want to turn away from it — whether the cause is something you see, smell, hear, taste, or witness in someone's behavior or character.
13249:
When we say someone or something is reputable, we mean they are known and respected for being good, honest, and trustworthy — especially within a particular field or community.

The word lives and dies on one concept: reputation. A person's reputation is what other people generally think and say about them based on their consistent behavior over time. If that reputation is a good one — built on honesty, quality, and reliability — then that person or thing is reputable.

Think of it this way: reputable = having a reputation worth respecting.

For someone or something to earn the label reputable, three ingredients usually need to be present:

1. Consistency over time. A single good act doesn't make you reputable. Reputation is built slowly, through repeated trustworthy behavior. A doctor who has practiced ethically for 20 years is reputable. A new clinic that just opened — even if it seems fine — hasn't yet earned that word.

2. Recognition by others. Reputation is not self-declared. You don't decide you're reputable — other people, through their experience and word-of-mouth, decide it for you. If a car mechanic is reputable, it's because customers and the wider community recognize and vouch for their honesty.

3. Being good at what they do AND being honest about it. Reputable combines competence (they do their job well) with integrity (they behave honestly and ethically). A skilled surgeon who overcharges patients dishonestly would not be called reputable. A helpful, honest advisor who isn't very knowledgeable might also fall short. You generally need both.

Reputable can describe several kinds of things:

  • People — a reputable lawyer, a reputable scientist
  • Businesses/Organizations — a reputable company, a reputable charity
  • Publications or Sources — a reputable journal, a reputable news outlet
  • Institutions — a reputable university, a reputable hospital
  • Brands or Products — a reputable manufacturer

In every case, the meaning is the same: this entity has earned genuine trust and respect from the people who know about it.

Reputable is a moderately strong word. It is a solid, real compliment — but it isn't the highest possible praise. Here's a rough sense of the ladder:

  • Reputable → trustworthy, well-regarded, respected (solid and reliable)
  • Highly reputable → exceptionally well-regarded
  • Prestigious → at the top, often implying fame and elite status

So calling a school "reputable" means: you can trust this school; it's known for doing things right. Calling it "prestigious" would mean it's at the very top, possibly world-famous. Reputable is grounded and practical; prestigious is more glamorous.

Understanding what a word doesn't mean is just as important.

  • Reputable ≠ Famous. A small, little-known law firm in a small town can be reputable if the local community deeply trusts it. Fame and reputation are different things. Fame is about how many people know you. Reputation is about what they know you for.
  • Reputable ≠ Perfect. It doesn't mean flawless. A reputable company may still make occasional mistakes — what matters is that they handle things honestly and have a consistent track record of good behavior.
  • Reputable ≠ Expensive or fancy. A budget hotel can be reputable. An affordable plumber can be reputable. The word has nothing to do with price or appearance.

The direct opposite is disreputable — meaning having a bad reputation; known for dishonesty, poor quality, or unethical behavior. A disreputable lender, for example, might trick customers with hidden fees or dishonest contracts.

Other words that express the opposite: shady, untrustworthy, dubious, sketchy (informal).
Words Close in Meaning (and How They Differ)

• Credible — focuses specifically on being believable and trustworthy as a source of information. A credible witness. A reputable witness would carry the extra meaning of also being generally well-regarded.
  • Reliable — focuses on dependability. Your old car might be reliable (it always starts), but we wouldn't call a car "reputable." Reliable is about performance; reputable is about earned social standing.
  • Respectable — very close to reputable, but slightly broader. Respectable can describe behavior or appearance ("he dressed in a respectable manner"), while reputable almost always refers to an entity's standing in the eyes of a community.
  • Trustworthy — focuses purely on honesty and reliability in keeping trust. Reputable includes this, but also includes the element of being publicly known for it.
  • Established — describes something that has existed for a long time and is recognized. An established brand is often reputable, but "established" alone doesn't guarantee good ethics — it just means longevity.
How It's Used in Real Sentences

• "Before hiring a contractor, make sure they are reputable — ask for references and check online reviews."

Here, reputable means: known in the community for honest, quality work.

  • "She only cites reputable sources in her research papers."

Here, reputable means: academically recognized and trustworthy; not random blogs or unreliable websites.

  • "We chose a reputable adoption agency to ensure the process was handled ethically."

Here, reputable means: well-known for doing things the right way, with integrity.

  • "The investment firm had a reputable history of transparent dealings with its clients."

Here, reputable describes a track record of trustworthy behavior over time.

When someone calls a person or organization reputable, the tone is calm, grounded, and confident. It's not gushing praise — it's more like a dependable endorsement. If a friend tells you, "Go to that clinic — it's reputable," they're saying: you can trust them; I'm confident they'll treat you right. It's reassurance rooted in evidence.
Reputable means: genuinely trusted and well-regarded by others, because of a consistent record of honesty, quality, and ethical behavior.
13250:
Repute means the opinion that people in general hold about someone or something — what a person, place, or organization is known for or thought to be like, in the eyes of others.

Think of it this way: your repute is not what you think of yourself. It is what the world thinks of you, based on what it has seen, heard, or come to believe over time.

A surgeon with decades of flawless work has a repute for precision and care.
A restaurant that has been serving bad food for years has a repute for poor quality.

In both cases, the repute did not come from one moment. It built up gradually, through the steady accumulation of how others experienced and talked about that person or place.
The Key Idea: It Lives in Other People's Minds

This is the single most important thing to understand about "repute." It does not live inside you — it lives outside you, in the minds of others. You can influence it through your actions, but you cannot simply declare it yourself. Other people decide it, hold it, and pass it on.

This is why a person can be wrongly accused and suffer a damaged repute — even if the truth is on their side, what others believe is what shapes repute.

Repute can lean in either direction:

Positive repute — being thought of well, with respect or admiration.

The university is of good repute and attracts students from across the world.
She is a writer of considerable repute in literary circles.

Negative repute — being thought of poorly, with suspicion or disapproval.

That neighborhood was once a place of ill repute, known for crime and disorder.
The company fell into bad repute after the scandal broke out.

"Of ill repute" is a particularly fixed and common phrase. You will encounter it often. It simply means: having a bad reputation, typically one associated with moral wrongdoing or disgraceful behavior. Historically, a "house of ill repute" was a polite way of saying a brothel.

This is one of the most useful and distinctive ways "repute" is used as a noun.

"By repute" means: according to what people generally say or believe, though not necessarily verified personally.

He is, by repute, the finest chess player in the country — though I have never seen him play myself.
The castle is, by repute, haunted.

Notice the slight distance in this phrase. When you say something "by repute," you are signaling that you are passing on the common belief — you are not personally vouching for it. It is like saying, "This is what people say." It can be true, it can be exaggerated, or it can even be a myth — but it is what repute holds.

• "of high repute" — greatly respected, held in very high regard.
  • "of some repute" — reasonably well known or respected, though not enormously famous.
  • "of international / national repute" — recognized and respected beyond a local circle, on a wider stage.
  • "held in high repute" — a slightly more formal way of saying someone is greatly respected.
  • "damage one's repute" — to harm the opinion others hold of someone.

Since you will certainly encounter both words, it is worth knowing how they relate.

They share the same core meaning. "Reputation" is the everyday, all-purpose word. "Repute" is the more formal, more literary version of the same idea. In casual speech and writing, people almost always use "reputation." "Repute," however, appears frequently in formal, legal, journalistic, or academic writing.

There is also a slight practical difference in how they appear in sentences:

  • "Reputation" is happy standing on its own: "She has a great reputation."
  • "Repute" tends to live more comfortably inside set phrases: "a doctor of good repute," "by repute," "of ill repute."

You would rarely say "She has a great repute" on its own — it sounds awkward. But "She is a doctor of great repute" sounds perfectly natural and elegant.
The Register: Who Uses This Word and When?

"Repute" is a formal word. You are more likely to read it than hear it in conversation. It appears in:

  • Legal language — "a person of good repute" in contracts or professional licensing
  • Journalism — describing public figures or institutions
  • Academic or professional writing — discussing organizations, experts, or establishments
  • Literature — especially older or more carefully crafted prose

If a friend calls you on the phone, they will almost certainly say "reputation," not "repute." But if you are reading a newspaper profile, a formal letter of recommendation, or a legal document, "repute" fits naturally.

"Repute" (noun) is the collective, general opinion that the world holds about a person, organization, or place — what they are known for, what they are believed to be, in the judgment of others. It is built over time, lives outside the person it describes, and can be positive or negative. As a noun, it appears most comfortably in fixed phrases like of good repute, of ill repute, and by repute. It is the formal, literary cousin of the everyday word "reputation," and it carries exactly the same essential meaning — just with a more refined, composed tone.
13251: A requiem is a solemn tribute to the dead — specifically, a prayer, ceremony, or piece of music offered for the peace and rest of a person's soul after they have died. The word always carries a mood of deep mourning, solemnity, and reverence. That is its emotional core. Everything else below is just that core idea appearing in different settings.

In the Catholic Church, a Requiem Mass (often simply called "a requiem") is a special church service held for someone who has died. It is not quite the same as a general funeral service. It is a specific, formal type of Mass — a sacred church ceremony — whose entire purpose is to pray for the soul of the deceased, asking God to grant them eternal rest and peace. The tone is deeply solemn and serious. It is not a cheerful "celebration of life"; it is a reverent, quiet act of prayer on behalf of the dead. This is where the word originates and where its meaning is purest.

Over the centuries, composers began writing large-scale music specifically designed to be sung during this Mass. This music itself came to be called "a requiem." So when someone says "Mozart wrote a requiem," they mean Mozart composed a major musical work — typically written for a choir, vocal soloists, and an orchestra — that was created to be performed during, or in the spirit of, a Mass for the dead.

Today, a requiem as a musical piece exists both as a religious work performed in a church and as a concert work performed in a concert hall. You don't need to be at a funeral to experience one. Some of the most celebrated requiems in history are Mozart's Requiem (which he left unfinished at the time of his death), Verdi's Requiem, Brahms' "A German Requiem," and Fauré's Requiem. Each composer brings a deeply personal voice to the form, which is why these pieces can sound remarkably different from one another — some are thunderous and dramatic, others are gentle and consoling — but they all share the same underlying purpose: to honor and mourn the dead through music.

Outside of religion and music, "requiem" is also used in a broader, metaphorical sense to describe anything — a speech, an article, a film, a final gesture — that acts as a last tribute or farewell to someone or something that is gone. It carries the same emotional weight as before: mourning, finality, and quiet respect.

For example: "The journalist's final article was a requiem for a way of life that had vanished." Or: "The closing ceremony felt like a requiem for everything the team had built together." Notice that in this figurative sense, the word doesn't have to refer to a person who has literally died. It can describe the end of an era, a place, a relationship, or an idea — anything that has permanently passed. What never changes is the feeling: something is gone, it mattered, and this moment honors that.
The One Thing That Never Changes

Across all three uses — religious, musical, and figurative — the word "requiem" always signals the same emotional register: something or someone has been lost, and what you are witnessing is a serious, careful, loving act of farewell. It is never a casual or lighthearted word. It belongs to the language of grief, memory, and deep respect. Whenever you encounter it, in any context, you can be sure the moment is a heavy one — something final is being acknowledged and honored.
13252:
When something is requisite, it means it is necessary and required for a specific purpose, situation, or standard. It is not just helpful or useful — it is genuinely needed. If something is requisite, you simply cannot properly do, complete, or achieve the thing in question without it.

Think of it this way: if you want to bake a cake, flour is requisite. You can experiment with other ingredients, but without flour, you don't have a cake at all. The flour is not optional. It is requisite.
The Key Idea Hidden Inside the Word

The most important thing to understand about requisite is that the "requirement" doesn't come from a person's personal preference or desire — it comes from the nature of the situation itself, or from an external standard, rule, or purpose.

For example:

  • A pilot must have the requisite training before flying a plane. It's not that an airline prefers trained pilots — the very nature of the job demands it.
  • A doctor must have the requisite qualifications to practice medicine. The law and the profession set that standard; it is non-negotiable.
  • To speak confidently in a foreign country, you need the requisite language skills. Without them, you simply cannot function in that environment.

In each case, the requirement exists because of a purpose, a standard, or a situation — not because of someone's personal wish.

Requisite carries a slightly formal, serious tone. You won't usually hear it in casual conversation. You're more likely to see or hear it in professional, academic, legal, or official contexts. When someone uses the word requisite, they are subtly signaling that the requirement they are speaking about is legitimate, objective, and important — not arbitrary.

It also often implies a minimum threshold — the baseline that must be met. Saying someone "has the requisite experience" means they have at least enough experience to qualify, to proceed, or to be taken seriously.
How It Sits in a Sentence

Requisite is always used before a noun in its adjective form. Here is the pattern:

the requisite + noun

Some natural examples:

  • She submitted the requisite paperwork before the deadline.
  • He didn't have the requisite confidence to speak in front of the crowd.
  • To get the job, you must demonstrate the requisite skills.
  • The student lacked the requisite knowledge to pass the exam.
  • They completed every step with the requisite care and precision.

Notice that in every case, removing "the requisite" and replacing it with "the necessary" or "the required" would give almost the same meaning — but requisite sounds more formal, more precise, and slightly more authoritative.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Understanding where requisite sits among similar words will sharpen your understanding of it significantly.

Necessary is the most general word. It simply means "needed." It works in almost any context, formal or informal. Requisite is a more formal and slightly more precise version of necessary, often implying that the standard comes from outside — from a rule, a purpose, or a field.

Required is direct and clear — something that a rule, authority, or process demands. Requisite is close to this but feels slightly less bureaucratic and slightly more elegant. "Required documents" and "requisite documents" mean roughly the same thing, but the latter sounds more formal and polished.

Essential suggests that something is fundamentally important — even critical — to the core of something. Requisite focuses more on whether a standard or threshold is met, while essential focuses more on deep importance.

Mandatory means something is compulsory — enforced by law, rule, or authority. You must do it or face a consequence. Requisite does not necessarily carry a threat or enforcement; it simply states that something is needed for a purpose to be fulfilled properly.
A Way to Test Your Understanding

Whenever you encounter the word requisite, ask yourself two quick questions:

  1. Required for what? — There is always a purpose, goal, or standard that the requisite thing is needed for. Find it.
  2. Who or what sets the requirement? — It's usually a situation, a profession, a rule, or the very nature of the task — not a personal preference.

If you can answer those two questions in context, you fully understand how the word is being used.

Requisite, as an adjective, means necessary and required to meet a specific standard, fulfill a purpose, or make something work properly. It is a formal word that signals the requirement is legitimate and objective — not optional, not preferential. It typically refers to a minimum threshold that must be met: the qualifications, skills, documents, conditions, or care that a situation genuinely demands. Used before a noun, it points directly at whatever it is that cannot be missing if the goal is to be achieved.
13253:
A requisition is a formal, official request — usually written — made to obtain something that is needed. But it's not just any ordinary request. What makes a requisition special is that it carries authority and weight behind it. It typically happens within an organization, institution, or government system, and it follows an established, recognized process.

Think of it this way: when you ask a friend to lend you a pen, that's just a request. But when a hospital manager fills out an official form to obtain 200 syringes from the medical supply department, that is a requisition. The difference is formality, authority, and process.
The Two Main Things a "Requisition" Can Mean

1. The Act of Formally Requesting Something

A requisition refers to the official act of asking for something — particularly goods, materials, equipment, or services — through a proper, authorized channel. This is extremely common in workplaces, the military, and government.

For example:

  • A soldier's unit puts in a requisition for more fuel and ammunition before a mission.
  • A school principal submits a requisition for 30 new textbooks.
  • An office manager files a requisition for a new printer.

In all these cases, the person isn't just casually asking. They are going through an official system to formally request what they need, often because they have the recognized authority or need to justify and document the request.

2. The Written Document Itself

A requisition is also the name of the actual physical or digital form/document used to make such a request. So the word refers both to the action and the paperwork involved.

For example:

  • "Please fill out a requisition before taking any equipment from the storeroom."
  • "The manager approved the requisition and sent it to the procurement department."

Here, the requisition is the form you fill out. It typically includes details like what you need, how many, why you need it, who is requesting it, and the date.
The Deeper Shade of Meaning: Authority and the Right to Demand

Here is where requisition becomes a richer word than simple "request." In more serious or powerful contexts — especially military, wartime, or governmental — a requisition is not merely asking. It is a formal, authoritative demand, sometimes backed by legal power, where the requesting party essentially has the right to take or use what they are claiming.

For example:

  • During a war, a government might issue a requisition for private citizens' vehicles or land to support the military effort. This isn't a polite ask — it is an official claim with authority. The citizens are expected to comply.
  • A court might issue a requisition for certain documents to be handed over.

So in these contexts, the word carries a sense of compulsion — the person or authority making the requisition doesn't just want something, they are formally asserting their right to have it.

You may occasionally come across the phrase "in requisition," which means something is in great demand or constantly being called upon and used.

For example:

  • "The community hall was in constant requisition during the festival season."

This just means the hall was being requested and used all the time. This usage is less common today but worth knowing.

No matter the context, a requisition always involves these core elements:

Formality — it's not casual or verbal; it follows a procedure.
Authority — it comes from or is directed to someone with recognized power or responsibility.
A clear need — it exists to obtain something specific: goods, services, materials, property, or information.
Documentation — it is typically recorded, written, or filed.
How Requisition Differs from Similar Words

Request is the broadest and most casual word. Anyone can make a request at any time with no special process. A requisition is a specific kind of request — more formal, more official, and more structured.

Order implies the transaction is already decided and is being commanded. A requisition is still a formal asking, even if it carries authority.

Demand sounds aggressive or forceful in everyday language. A requisition is also firm and authoritative, but it works within a system — it's procedural and dignified rather than confrontational.

Application is a formal request too, but usually made by an outsider (like applying for a job or a permit). A requisition is typically made within a system — by someone who already belongs to the organization or has established authority.
Everyday Examples to Cement the Idea

• A nurse fills out a requisition for extra medical gloves from the hospital's supply room.
  • A field commander submits a requisition for helicopter support.
  • A teacher sends in a requisition for art supplies for the upcoming semester.
  • A wartime government issues a requisition for all privately owned radio equipment in the country.
  • An IT department receives a requisition for 10 new laptops from the marketing team.

In short, a requisition is an official, formal request — and sometimes a formal demand — made through a recognized process, usually documented in writing, most commonly seen in organizational, military, and governmental settings. It is the word that sits right at the border between asking and officially claiming, depending on how much authority is behind it.
13254:
Requital means giving back something in return for what someone has done to you. Think of it as the act of balancing the scales — if someone does something for you (or to you), and you respond by giving them something back in return, that response is the requital.

The key thing to understand is that requital works in both directions — it can be a repayment of something good, or a repayment of something bad. This is what makes it a rich and precise word.

When someone shows you love, kindness, loyalty, or a good deed, and you respond by giving the same back, that is a requital of their goodness. For example, if a friend stood by you during the hardest years of your life and you later devoted yourself to caring for them in their old age, your devotion is a requital of their friendship. You are returning what was given to you.

This positive meaning often carries a sense of warmth and moral fairness — a sense that goodness deserves to be answered with goodness.

Requital equally applies when the original act was harmful. If someone betrays you, hurts you, or wrongs you, and you respond by making them feel the consequences of that — whether through punishment, revenge, or justice — that too is requital. A person who was cheated by a business partner and later exposes them publicly has enacted a requital of the wrong done to them.

In this darker sense, requital is close in feeling to revenge or retribution, but it is a calmer, more neutral word. It simply means the return of harm for harm, without necessarily judging whether that return was righteous or excessive.

What unites both sides — the kind requital and the harsh requital — is this: requital is always a response, never a first action. It is always triggered by something that came before it. Something happens first, and requital is what follows as a deliberate return. Without that original act, there is no requital. This is what separates it from random acts of kindness or random cruelty — requital is always answering something.

Requital is a formal, literary word. You will not hear it in casual conversation — you are far more likely to encounter it in classic literature, poetry, formal writing, or speeches. In everyday speech, people would say "payback," "repayment," "revenge," or "returning the favor" depending on the situation. Requital covers all of these, but with a more dignified and serious tone.
How it differs from similar words

Retaliation is only negative — it always means striking back against harm. Requital can be positive or negative.

Gratitude is the feeling of thankfulness. Requital is the action of paying that thankfulness back. You can feel gratitude without offering requital; requital is when you actually do something about it.

Reward is something given by a person in a position of authority or advantage. Requital is more personal and mutual — it is about you responding to what was done specifically to you.

Compensation is usually about money or practical redress. Requital can be emotional, moral, or relational — it is far broader.

You will often see requital used in the phrase "in requital of" something. This simply means "as a return for" or "in response to." For example: "She gave her life in requital of the sacrifice he had made for her" means she gave her life because of and in response to his sacrifice — as a way of honoring and repaying it.

"He asked for no requital — he had helped her simply because it was right."
(He wanted nothing back in return for his help.)

"The destruction of his village was a requital for years of oppression that his people had suffered."
(The destruction was their answer — their payback — for what had been done to them.)

"She showered him with kindness in requital of his loyalty during her darkest years."
(She gave him kindness back because of the loyalty he had shown her.)
The single sentence that captures everything

If you ever need to recall this word quickly, remember this: requital is the act of giving back — whether good for good, or harm for harm — in response to what someone has done to you. It is the completion of a moral or emotional circle.
13255:
To requite something means to return a feeling, action, or treatment that someone gave you first. It's about giving back — matching what you received.

Think of it as completing a circle. Someone starts the circle by doing something to you or feeling something for you. When you requite it, you complete that circle by giving something back in return.

The word works in both positive and negative situations.

Positive — returning love, kindness, or a good deed:

When someone loves you and you love them back, you requite their love. When someone shows you loyalty and you are loyal to them in return, you requite their loyalty.

"He had loved her for years, and she finally requited his feelings."
(= She finally loved him back.)

"She requited every act of kindness he had shown her."
(= She paid back his kindness with kindness of her own.)

Negative — returning harm, betrayal, or cruelty:

You can also requite something bad — a wrong done to you, an insult, or a betrayal. In this sense, it means to pay someone back for the harm they caused, similar to retaliation or revenge.

"He requited their treachery by cutting all ties with them."
(= He paid them back for their betrayal.)

"She requited his cruelty with cold indifference."
(= She responded to his cruelty with deliberate coldness.)
The Key Ingredient: It Must Be Intentional

Requiting is always a deliberate, conscious act. You choose to return what you received. It's never accidental. There's a sense of fairness or balance behind it — making things even, whether through returned affection or returned punishment.

The word you will most commonly encounter in real life is unrequited — the negative form, meaning "not returned."

Unrequited love is love that one person feels strongly but the other person does not return. The circle never gets completed.

"His love was unrequited — she simply did not feel the same way."

So if you ever see or hear "unrequited," now you know it literally means: the requiting (the returning) never happened.

You can requite a person or a thing:

  • Requite a person → you are paying them back (for something they did)
    • "She requited him for his generosity." (She paid him back for being generous.)
  • Requite a feeling or action → you are returning that specific thing
    • "He never requited her affection." (He never returned her affection.)
The Register: When and Where Is This Word Used?

Requite is a formal, literary word. You would not hear it in casual everyday speech. It lives in literature, poetry, formal writing, and careful, educated conversation. If you said "I will requite your kindness" in a conversation, it would sound elevated and poetic, not odd — but definitely not casual.

The adjective form unrequited is far more common in everyday use than the verb itself, almost always paired with love, feelings, or affection.
To requite means to return — deliberately and in full — a feeling, action, or treatment that someone gave you first, whether that return is warm (love, kindness) or cold (revenge, punishment).
13256:
To rescind something means to officially cancel, withdraw, or take back a decision, agreement, law, or order that was previously made — as if it never existed or as if it no longer holds any power.

Think of it this way: when you rescind something, you are undoing an official act. You put something into place, and now you are pulling it back out.
The Key Idea: It Has to Be Something "Official"

This is the most important thing to understand about "rescind." You don't rescind casual, everyday things. You rescind things that carry formal authority or weight — things like:

  • A law or regulation
  • A job offer
  • A contract
  • A policy
  • An order or decree
  • A decision made by a committee, court, or organization
  • A membership or license

So if you told your friend you'd meet them for lunch and then changed your mind, you wouldn't say you rescinded your plan. But if a company sent you a formal job offer letter and then officially withdrew it, they rescinded the offer.

• The government rescinded the law after massive public protests. (The law was cancelled.)
  • The university rescinded her admission after discovering she had lied on her application. (The admission was officially taken back.)
  • The board rescinded its earlier decision and voted again. (They cancelled their previous decision.)
  • After the scandal, his security clearance was rescinded. (It was officially revoked.)

When something is rescinded, it stops being valid or enforceable. The act of rescinding doesn't just pause or freeze something — it eliminates its power and effect. In legal and formal settings especially, rescinding something often means treating it as though it should no longer be recognized or acted upon going forward.

Imagine a government passes a rule. That rule has power — people must follow it. The moment the government rescinds that rule, it loses its power. Done. Gone.

Rescinding often carries a sense of reversal and sometimes consequence. It's not a light or casual action. When something is rescinded, it usually means:

  • Something went wrong (e.g., fraud, a mistake, new circumstances), or
  • Someone in power deliberately changed course, or
  • A situation changed so significantly that the original decision no longer makes sense

So there's usually a reason behind a rescission, and it often affects people in significant ways (you lose a job offer, a law stops applying, a contract dissolves).
How It Differs from Similar Words

Since you want to know this word deeply, it helps to understand how it sits among similar words:

  • Cancel is the broad, everyday word. You can cancel a pizza order, a meeting, a show. Rescind is more formal and specific to official acts.
  • Revoke is very close in meaning and often interchangeable with rescind. However, revoke tends to be used when taking back a privilege or right given to a person (a driver's license is revoked, a permit is revoked). Rescind is broader and more commonly used for decisions, laws, orders, and contracts.
  • Repeal is specifically used for laws and legislation. A law is repealed through a legislative process. While you can also say a law is rescinded, repeal is the more precise legal term for that narrow case.
  • Annul typically means to declare something legally void from the beginning — as though it never existed (commonly used for marriages or contracts). Rescind is similar but doesn't always imply it was invalid from the start — it just means it is being cancelled now.
  • Withdraw is softer and more general. You withdraw an offer in a casual or early-stage sense. Rescind is the formal, official version of withdrawal.

In real life, you'll most often see "rescind" paired with these words:

  • Rescind an offer (especially a job offer)
  • Rescind a contract
  • Rescind a law or policy
  • Rescind an order (executive order, court order)
  • Rescind a decision
  • Rescind approval or authorization
  • Rescind membership or accreditation

To rescind = to officially cancel or take back a formal decision, agreement, or rule, stripping it of its power or validity.

If you remember that one line and the idea that it always involves something official, you'll use and understand this word correctly every single time.
13257:
Rescission is the act of officially canceling, wiping out, or undoing an agreement, contract, or law — in such a way that it is treated as though it never existed in the first place.

That phrase — "never existed in the first place" — is the absolute heart of this word. Rescission doesn't simply end something and move on. It erases the thing going backward in time, restoring everyone involved to the exact position they were in before the agreement ever happened.
The Big Idea: Turning Back the Clock

Think of it this way. Imagine you and a friend make a deal. You give him your bike, and he gives you $200. Later, you discover he lied to you to make the deal happen. A regular cancellation would say, "The deal is over — you keep your money and I keep my bike." But rescission goes further and says: "This deal is being erased. It never legally happened. Give me my bike back, and I'll give you your $200 back. We are back to square one."

This "return to square one" quality is what makes rescission different from almost every other word that involves ending or canceling something. It is retroactive — meaning it acts backward, not just forward.

Rescission is most commonly used in three areas:

1. Contract Law (the most common use)

In everyday legal life, rescission is used to completely undo a contract. When a contract is rescinded, it is voided from the very beginning — lawyers call this void ab initio, meaning "void from the start." Any goods exchanged must be returned, any money paid must be refunded, and any work done may need to be compensated, so that no one is left worse off than before the contract existed.

2. Real Estate

Rescission is especially important in property transactions. In many countries, when you sign a contract to buy a home, you are legally given a short window of time — often called a "rescission period" or "cooling-off period" — during which you can change your mind, cancel the purchase contract, and get your deposit back. The contract is treated as though it was never signed. This protects buyers from making rushed decisions on one of the biggest purchases of their lives.

3. Laws and Government Orders

Rescission is also used when a government, court, or authority formally cancels a law, regulation, order, or decision. For example, a government might pass a rescission of a previous policy, meaning that policy is officially withdrawn and no longer has any force — as if it were struck off the books.

A contract or agreement is not rescinded randomly. There must be a valid legal reason. The most recognized reasons include:

Fraud — One party deliberately lied or deceived the other to get them to sign. If you buy a car and the seller secretly knew the engine was broken and lied about it, that is fraud, and you may be entitled to rescission.

Misrepresentation — Similar to fraud, but the false statement may have been made without intent to deceive. Even an honest but incorrect statement that caused you to enter a contract can be grounds for rescission.

Mistake — Both parties were operating under a fundamental misunderstanding of the key facts at the time the contract was made. If both a buyer and seller believed a painting was an original masterpiece but it turned out to be a forgery, and that belief was the entire reason the contract existed, rescission could apply.

Duress or Undue Influence — If someone was forced, threatened, or manipulated into signing an agreement, they did not give true free consent. Contracts entered under duress can be rescinded because genuine agreement never really existed.

Lack of Capacity — If a person was legally incapable of entering a contract at the time — for example, they were a minor, or mentally incapacitated — rescission can undo that agreement.

Failure of Consideration — "Consideration" in contract law means what each party gives in exchange (money, goods, services, a promise). If one party completely fails to deliver what they promised, the other party may be able to seek rescission.
Rescission vs. Termination: A Crucial Distinction

These two words are often confused, so it is worth making the difference crystal clear.

Termination ends a contract going forward from a certain point. Everything that happened before termination remains legally valid. If you hired someone for a year, paid them for six months, and then terminated the contract, those six months of payments and work stand — the contract just stops now.

Rescission goes further and says the contract was defective from birth. It is not just ended; it is annulled. It is as if it was never formed. The goal is to undo everything, returning all parties to their original positions. This is why courts take rescission very seriously — it is a much more powerful and complete remedy than simple termination.

A helpful way to remember this: termination is like closing a book at chapter six. Rescission is like shredding the book and pretending it was never written.

Mutual Rescission happens when both parties to a contract voluntarily and jointly agree to cancel it. They both want out. In this case, they simply agree that the contract is over and work out how to return things to the way they were. This is the most peaceful and straightforward form of rescission.

Unilateral Rescission is when only one party wants to cancel the contract, and they do so on legal grounds (such as fraud or misrepresentation). The other party may or may not agree. In these cases, the matter often ends up before a court, which then decides whether rescission is legally warranted.

Rescission can be granted in two ways:

By agreement between the parties (mutual rescission, as described above), without needing a court.

By a court or legal authority, when one party applies for rescission and the court rules in their favor based on legal grounds like fraud or duress.

Once rescission is granted or agreed upon, the legal doctrine of restitution kicks in. Restitution means restoring each party to their original position. Money is refunded. Property is returned. Any unjust enrichment — meaning any benefit one party unfairly gained from the other through the flawed contract — must be given back. The law tries to make it as though the contract simply never happened.
A Quick Real-World Example to Tie It All Together

You sign a contract to buy a piece of land for $50,000. You pay the money and the deal closes. Later, you discover that the seller had a legal obligation to tell you the land was contaminated, and they deliberately hid this from you — that is fraud.

You go to court and seek rescission of the contract. The court agrees. The contract is declared void from the very beginning. The seller must give you back your $50,000. You must give back the land. Neither party profits from the fraudulent deal. You are both, as closely as possible, returned to where you stood before any of it happened.

That entire process — the legal undoing of that contract from its root — is rescission.
Rescission is the complete legal cancellation of a contract, law, or agreement that wipes it out as if it never existed, restoring all parties to their original position before it was made.
13258:
A rescript is an official written reply issued by a supreme authority — such as a ruler, emperor, or the Pope — in direct response to a formal question, petition, or legal inquiry submitted to them. Think of it as a very powerful, formal written answer that carries the weight of law or binding authority.

The word is not used in casual everyday life. It belongs to the worlds of law, history, government, and religious administration.

Imagine you are living under an emperor's rule, and you have a legal dispute you can't resolve. Ordinary courts are stumped. So you write a formal petition directly to the emperor asking: "Your Majesty, what is the law in this situation?" The emperor reviews your case and writes back an official answer. That written answer — authoritative, formal, and binding — is a rescript.

The key things that make something a rescript are:

  • It comes from the highest authority (an emperor, a pope, a sovereign power).
  • It is a response — it only exists because someone first asked a question or submitted a petition.
  • It is written and official.
  • It carries binding or legal force, meaning it isn't just an opinion. It settles the matter.
The Two Main Contexts Where You'll Encounter This Word

1. Roman Law and Imperial Rescripts

This is the most historically important use of the word. In ancient Rome, one of the primary ways Roman emperors created law was through rescripts. Judges, governors, magistrates, and even private citizens could write to the emperor asking for a legal ruling on a specific situation. The emperor — or his legal advisors writing in his name — would study the question and issue a formal written reply.

This reply, the rescript, was then treated as the authoritative interpretation of the law for that case, and often served as a legal precedent that guided future cases as well. Hundreds of these imperial rescripts were collected and preserved in great Roman legal compilations, like the Codex of Justinian, where they helped form the backbone of Roman law as we know it today.

So in this context, a rescript is both an act of governance and an act of lawmaking — the emperor speaking with full legal authority in writing.

2. The Catholic Church and Papal Rescripts

The second major context is the Catholic Church, which inherited much of its administrative structure from Roman traditions. Here, a rescript is an official written document issued by the Pope or another competent Church authority (such as a Vatican office) in response to a formal request or petition submitted by a person, a group, or even a bishop.

Rescripts in this context are used to:

  • Grant a dispensation (an exception from a Church rule or law for a specific person or situation, e.g., allowing a marriage that would normally be restricted by canon law).
  • Grant a privilege or special permission.
  • Provide an authoritative answer to a question of Church law or doctrine.

A rescript from the Pope does not just express a wish — it formally grants or decides something. It has legal standing within canon law (the internal law of the Catholic Church). Once issued, it creates a real, binding change in the legal situation of the person who petitioned for it.
An Analogy to Make It Click

Think of a rescript like a formal written ruling from a judge, but the "judge" here is the single most powerful authority in that world — the emperor of an empire or the head of the Church — and the ruling only came into being because someone first asked for it. It's the highest possible written response to a formal question, and it carries the force of law.

Contrast this with a decree or edict, which is issued on the authority's own initiative to address the general public. A rescript is reactive and specific — it answers a question directed at the authority.

It is always a response. This is fundamental. A rescript cannot exist without a prior petition or inquiry. If the authority issues something on their own initiative, that is a different kind of document (like an edict or decree). The reactive, responsive nature of a rescript is what defines it.

It is specific, not general. Rescripts typically address the specific question or situation raised by the petitioner. While they can be used as precedent, they are not inherently meant to be broad laws for everyone.

It can be misused. Historically, people sometimes obtained rescripts by providing false information in their petition. Roman and Church law both recognized this problem. A rescript obtained through deceit or misrepresentation was considered invalid — the authority's reply was only binding if it was based on accurate information.

The word can be used more loosely. In some literary or historical contexts, "rescript" is used more broadly to mean any kind of official restatement, revised directive, or formal written response from a government authority — not necessarily from the very top. But when used precisely, it refers to the specific Roman/legal/canonical tradition described above.

A rescript is a formal, authoritative, written response issued by a supreme power — classically a Roman emperor or the Pope — to a specific question or petition directed at them. It has the force of law or binding authority within its domain. It is defined by three things: it comes from the top, it responds to a specific request, and it is written. You'll encounter this word most often in discussions of Roman law, legal history, and Catholic canon law.
13259:
At the heart of every meaning of reservation is one simple idea: setting something aside, or holding something back — keeping it separate from everything else.

Whether you're talking about a table at a restaurant, a doubt in your mind, or a stretch of land, something is being kept, held, or withheld for a specific purpose or reason.
Meaning 1: A Booking or Arrangement (Most Common)

When you contact a hotel, restaurant, airline, or any service and ask them to keep something for you at a future time, you are making a reservation. The reservation is the arrangement itself — the confirmed promise that something will be held for you.

"I'd like to make a reservation for two at 7 PM."
"Do you have a reservation under the name Singh?"
"I lost my reservation confirmation email."

What's being "set aside" here is a physical spot, a seat, a room, or a ticket — kept specifically for you, not given to anyone else until you arrive.

Key detail: A reservation is made in advance — before you actually use the thing. You reserve it now so it's waiting for you later. Once you've actually used the service (you've eaten the meal, checked out of the hotel), the word "reservation" no longer applies to that transaction.

Common collocations:

  • make a reservation
  • hold a reservation
  • cancel a reservation
  • confirm a reservation
  • reservation number / reservation code
  • hotel/restaurant/flight reservation
Meaning 2: A Doubt, Hesitation, or Concern

When you are not fully comfortable agreeing with something — when some part of your mind says "wait, but..." — you have a reservation.

"I support the plan, but I have reservations about the timeline."
"She accepted the offer without reservation." (meaning: without any doubt at all, completely)
"He had serious reservations about trusting her."

Here, "reservation" means something you are withholding — specifically, your full, unconditional agreement. Part of your consent is being held back.

Notice that this meaning almost always appears in the plural ("reservations") when you're expressing doubt. The singular "reservation" is more common in phrases like "without reservation" (meaning completely, wholeheartedly).

Nuance: A reservation is gentler than a flat-out objection. If you have a reservation, you're not saying "no." You're saying "yes, but..." — you're leaning toward agreement while something still nags at you.

Common collocations:

  • have reservations (about something)
  • without reservation
  • express reservations
  • deep/serious reservations
  • voice/share one's reservations
Meaning 3: A Piece of Land Set Aside for a Specific Group or Purpose

In certain formal or official contexts, a reservation is an area of land that has been officially designated — separated from surrounding land — for a particular group of people or a specific use.

The most prominent use: In the United States and Canada, a reservation (also called a "reserve" in Canada) is land that the government has formally set aside for Indigenous/Native peoples to live on and govern. These are sovereign territories with their own laws and governance.

"The Navajo Reservation is the largest Native American reservation in the United States."
"He grew up on a reservation in South Dakota."

More broadly, land can also be "reserved" for nature and wildlife:

"a wildlife reservation" / "a nature reservation"

(though the word reserve is often preferred in these cases — "a nature reserve" — "reservation" is less common here but still used)

The idea is the same: land is set aside, separated from general use, and dedicated to something specific.
Meaning 4: A Condition, Qualification, or Exception

In formal writing and speech, a reservation can also refer to a specific limitation or exception attached to an agreement or statement — a condition you're keeping in mind even while broadly agreeing.

"The committee approved the proposal with certain reservations."
"I accept your argument, but with one reservation: the data is from 2015."

This is closely related to Meaning 2 (a doubt), but with a slightly more formal tone. Here, the reservation is almost like a written footnote — you're agreeing, but you're specifically carving out an exception or noting a limit to your agreement.

All four meanings come from the same underlying logic:

MeaningWhat is being "set aside" or "held back"?
BookingA physical spot, room, or seat
DoubtYour full, unconditional agreement
LandA geographical area
QualificationYour complete, exception-free acceptance

Actually, let me put that in plain words instead:

In a booking, a place or spot is set aside for you. In a doubt, your full agreement is being held back. On designated land, a territory is set apart. With a qualification, your complete acceptance is withheld. Every single time, something is being kept separate, held in reserve, not fully given over.
Common Phrases and Patterns Worth Knowing

"Without reservation" — completely, with no hesitation, no doubts whatsoever.

"I recommend her without reservation." (= I have zero doubts about recommending her.)

"Have reservations about" — to feel uncertain or uneasy about something.

"I have reservations about quitting my job so suddenly."

"Under reservation" — sometimes used to mean something is being held pending a confirmed booking (less common in everyday speech, more formal/legal).

"Make a reservation" — to book something in advance.

"Can you make a reservation at that new Italian place?"

• It is not the same as cancellation (that's when a reservation is ended or withdrawn).
  • It is not the same as a guarantee — a reservation can sometimes still be cancelled by either party.
  • It is not the same as a refusal — having reservations means hesitating, not outright saying no.
  • It is not the same as a preference — a reservation is a formal or official act of setting something aside, not just wanting something.

Reservation is a noun built around the idea of holding something apart — keeping it back from the general flow. In daily life, it most often means a booking (a table, a room, a seat held for you in advance). In your thoughts and feelings, it means a doubt or hesitation — the part of you that hasn't fully agreed yet. In geography and governance, it refers to land officially set aside for a specific community or purpose. And in formal language, it can mean a qualification or exception you're attaching to your agreement. The same word fits all four meanings because they all share the same core: something is reserved — separated, held, and not just given away freely.
13260: A reservoir is a place where a large amount of something — most often a liquid — is collected, held, and stored so that it can be used when needed. Think of it as a "savings account," but instead of money, it stores things like water, oil, or even ideas. The defining quality of a reservoir is that it acts as a supply that you draw from over time — it is not just a passing flow, but a stored body that stays put.

When most people say "reservoir," they mean a large body of stored water, usually meant to supply a city, town, or farming region.

Reservoirs of this kind come in two forms:

1. Man-made (artificial) reservoirs — These are the most common type. Humans build a dam across a river, which blocks the natural flow of water. As the water has nowhere to go, it backs up and collects, forming a huge lake behind the dam. That lake is the reservoir. Cities then pipe water from it for people to drink, cook with, and bathe in. A good example is the Hoover Dam on the Colorado River, which created Lake Mead — one of the largest reservoirs in the world.

2. Natural reservoirs — Sometimes, a natural lake or even a large underground layer of rock acts as a reservoir. The water simply gathered there over thousands of years on its own, and humans tap into it.

The key point is the purpose: a reservoir is not just any lake. It is water that is being managed and stored for a specific use.

A reservoir does not have to sit on the surface. Deep underground, porous rock (rock full of tiny holes, like a sponge) can be soaked with water, oil, or natural gas. These underground pockets of stored liquid or gas are also called reservoirs. When an oil company drills a well, they are drilling down to reach an oil reservoir — a layer of rock that has been holding oil for millions of years.

In the same way, underground water reservoirs (called aquifers) supply wells across the world. Many farms and rural homes depend entirely on water pumped up from these hidden reservoirs.

The word is also used for small containers inside machines or devices that store a liquid needed for the machine to work.

For example:

  • A car has a brake fluid reservoir — a small plastic tank under the hood that stores the fluid needed to make the brakes work.
  • A fountain pen has an ink reservoir — the chamber inside the pen that holds the ink.
  • A car's windshield wiper system has a washer fluid reservoir.

In all these cases, the idea is the same: a dedicated holding space that stores a liquid so it is ready to be used as needed.

Because a reservoir suggests a large, deep, available supply, people also use the word figuratively — meaning they apply it to things that are not physical liquids at all.

You might hear or read sentences like:

  • "She has a deep reservoir of patience." — She has a great deal of patience stored within her, ready to be drawn on.
  • "The country has a vast reservoir of talent." — There are many talented people available in that country.
  • "His years of experience gave him a reservoir of knowledge." — He has accumulated so much knowledge that he can draw from it like water from a well.

In all these cases, the speaker is painting a picture: just as a water reservoir is a large, dependable store you can draw from, this person or place has a large, dependable store of something valuable.

In science, especially in medicine and biology, reservoir has a very specific meaning. It refers to a species, animal, or environment that permanently carries and harbors a disease-causing germ (like a virus or bacteria) without being seriously harmed by it itself.

For example, bats are considered a natural reservoir for certain viruses. The virus lives inside the bat population across generations. The bats generally do not get sick from it, but the virus can sometimes jump from bats to humans, causing outbreaks. In this sense, the bat population is the "storage place" for the virus — it is where the germ lives and waits, just like water waits in a dam.
What Ties All These Meanings Together

No matter which context you see the word "reservoir" in, three ideas are always present:

  1. Storage — Something is being held and kept, not just passing through.
  2. Quantity — There is a significant amount of whatever is being stored.
  3. Future use — The stored thing is being kept precisely because it will be needed and drawn from later.

If you remember these three ideas — stored, substantial, and available for use — you will understand the word "reservoir" correctly in any sentence you ever encounter it.
13261:
To reside somewhere means to live there as your home — in a settled, established way. It is not about visiting a place or passing through. It means that place is where you actually belong, sleep, and have made your life.

"She resides in Tokyo."

This means Tokyo is her home. She lives there. It is where her life is based.

"Reside" and "live" mean almost the same thing, but there is an important difference in tone and formality.

  • "Live" is the everyday, casual word. You use it in normal conversation.
  • "Reside" is the formal version. You see it in official documents, legal papers, news articles, and formal writing.

Think of it this way: you would say "Where do you live?" to a friend at a coffee shop. But a government form would ask "State the city where you currently reside."

Both sentences ask for the same information. The word "reside" just sounds more serious, official, and polished.

This is a critical distinction. "Reside" always implies permanence or long-term settlement. It is not temporary.

  • If you are at a hotel for three days → you are staying there, not residing.
  • If you are visiting your parents for a week → you are visiting, not residing.
  • If you moved to a city and that is now your home → you reside there.

The idea of roots, stability, and an established home is baked into the meaning of "reside." A person who resides somewhere has made it their base of life — not just a temporary stop.

Here is where "reside" becomes even more interesting. The word is also used beyond physical places. It can describe where a quality, a power, a feeling, or an idea "lives" — meaning where it exists or is found.

"True power resides in the people, not in the government."

This does not mean people literally live inside something. It means power belongs to, is located in, or is held by the people. The power has its "home" there.

More examples of this figurative use:

"The real problem resides in the way the system was designed."

→ The problem is found within the design itself.

"Wisdom does not reside in age alone."

→ Wisdom is not simply located in or guaranteed by old age.

"The final decision resides with the manager."

→ The authority to decide belongs to, and sits with, the manager.

In all these cases, think of "reside" as asking: "Where does this thing have its home? Where does it belong or exist?" — and then answering that question.

Reside is always followed by a preposition. The most common ones are:

  • reside in → used with cities, countries, buildings, or abstract things
    "He resides in Canada." / "The issue resides in the code."*
  • reside at → used with a specific address
    "She resides at 14 Elm Street."*
  • reside with → used when authority, power, or a right belongs to someone
    "The final say resides with the committee."*

Since you want to fully understand this word, knowing its family will help you recognize it in different forms:

  • Resident (noun) → a person who resides somewhere
    "She is a resident of New York."*
  • Residence (noun) → the place where someone resides; the act of residing
    "His residence is in the countryside." / "She took up residence in Rome."*
  • Residential (adjective) → relating to where people reside
    "This is a quiet, residential neighborhood."*
  • Residing (present participle) → the ongoing action
    "The family residing in that house has lived there for decades."*

DimensionDetail
Basic meaningTo live somewhere as your established home
ToneFormal — used in official, legal, and serious writing
Key ideaPermanence and settlement — not temporary
Figurative useWhere something (power, quality, problem) exists or belongs
Common prepositionsin, at, with

The single most important thing to remember: "reside" is the formal way of saying "live in a place as your home," and it can also describe where something non-physical — like power, truth, or a problem — is found or belongs.
13262:
Residue is whatever is left behind after most of something has been removed, used up, consumed, or processed.

Think of it this way — something happens to a substance or a whole, and when the main action is over, there's a leftover portion that wasn't fully dealt with. That leftover is the residue.

Residue always implies a before and after. Something existed in a fuller or original form. Then a process happened — burning, washing, evaporating, filtering, reacting, spending, time passing. What survives that process, often in a smaller or altered form, is the residue. It is fundamentally the remainder — what was not consumed, not removed, not transformed away.

It is almost always smaller in quantity than the original thing. You don't usually call the bigger portion the residue; you call the leftover the residue.

When you wash a greasy pan but don't scrub thoroughly, there's a thin film of grease still clinging to the surface. That's residue. When you drink a glass of juice and there's a sticky coating left inside the glass, that's residue. When pesticides are sprayed on crops and traces remain on the fruit you buy at the store, those traces are called pesticide residue. When you peel a sticker off a surface and there's that annoying sticky patch left behind, that's adhesive residue.

In all these cases, notice the pattern: a substance was there, something happened (washing, drinking, peeling), but a portion stubbornly remained. That remainder is the residue.

This is where the word is used most precisely and technically. In chemistry, residue refers to the solid or concentrated material that remains after a substance has undergone a process such as evaporation, combustion (burning), filtration, or a chemical reaction.

For example: if you boil saltwater until all the water evaporates, you are left with solid salt crystals. Those crystals are the residue. If you burn wood completely, the ash left behind is the residue of the combustion process. If you filter a liquid through a fine mesh, the solid particles that the filter catches and holds back — unable to pass through — are called the residue (or filter residue).
